A CONTINGENCY.—" What are you going to name the boy?" asked the old:neighbour. "We thought something of naming him after one of our states. men," answered the proud and happy father. "One of the dead ones, or one of the live ones?" "One of living ones." "Don't you do it! Don't you do it! It isn't safe. About the time you get the kid named for some politician you admire, the politician is likely to have gone clean over to the -party you detest." - • • - • - -

_ _ B.zesstraisa.—A tourist in Switzerland, who ,was about to make the ascent of a mountain, thought best to ask some questions as to the cap- abilities of his guide. "Is he a thoroughly skilful climber?" he asked of a hotel-keeper. "I should say so l" exclaimed the innkeeper. "He has lost two parties of tourists down the mountain side, and escaped without a scratch both times, PnovEla A FAILURE.—Her mother was die- appointed, and she did not hesitate to show '" Not a single proposal this summer," she said. "I know it, mamma," repeated the daughter, regretfully. "And your father and I did every- ' thing possible for you, too," continued the mother. "We got you a bicycle and the prettiest black silk bloomers to be seen at any of the summer resorts." " I know it, mamma," repeated the daughter, "but it was an error of judgment. Next summer I'll sell the bicycle and the bloomers, and buy a nice cosy hammock and dainty white lawn 'dress, and take my pick of all the men at the sea- shore. The bicycle girl attracts a lot of attention, but I've noticed that it's the hammock girl who gets married." INcomthiat..n. A man of this city who thoroughly loves a good cigar v,as indulging in a smoke after dinner, when a friend who is given to moralising touched him on the arm, and said: "I'm sorry that you still have that habit." "I'm mot," was the emphatic reply. "I was examined for life insurance yesterday, and the doctor says my health is first-rate. So there is no use in telling me that it is hurrying me into my grave, or the!.,e.9 don't bear out the assertion." "But it's a very expensive habit." "I find the satisfac- tion such as to make me content to foot the bill." "How long have you been smoking?" "Fifteen or twenty years." "Do you realise that with the money you have spent in that way yo.i might 'have laid the foundation for a fortune? Why, you 'might have been the owner of that block of houses over there." "I have heard that kind of argu- ment before, and it does not impress me. If I had bought them with money saved in that way I'd be miserable thinking of the good times I might have had smoking if I hadn't wasted my money on blocks of houses."
A LITTLE GIRL'S " IF."—Whoever has the sym- pathy which makes .one kin with children knows

- to vhat heights of fine and tender feeling the little ones, not excepting the most indefatigable tenfarat terrible, can easily rise. Enid never fails in her Bible lessons to demonstrate that there are *quick wits under her crown of golden curls. But a recent lesson on original sin rather daunted her; she failed, as some older doctrinarians have done, to solve the problem, but she applied thereto the teaching of "honour thy father and thy mother" in a spirit of faith which approached the sublime. Her mother explained that Eve's disobedience was a terrible and wicked thing—that Emid and her little brothers needed to try very hard to be good and to oppose the great sin and sorrow that had been in the world ever since Eve yielded to -temptation. &aid was sad and dissatisfied, then she exclaimed, in a tone of inconsolable regret: oh, mamma! If you had only .had Eve's chance!" _ _

Time was when members of the Tory party went about the country piously thanking God for the Ilouse of Lords. Mr. Healy on Monday evening astonished his colleagues by offering up a similar thanksgiving for the existence of the House of Commons. The provocation was the Evidence in Criminal Cases Bill—s. measure which the Lords have already passed, and which the Commons were now invited to read a second time. Its main pur- pose is to give prisoners the right of going. into the witness-box to offer sworn evidence on their own behalf. According to the Attorney-General, there are already twenty-six classes of offence in which the accused person may adopt this course. He and Sir Edward Clarke and many other eminent lawyers are in favour of extending the principle to all criminal trials. Mr.llealy does not agree with them, and thus it was that he came to bless the House of Commons as an obstacle to the revolutionary de- signs of the Peers: He made one good and interest- ing point by reminding members that when Mr. Parnell got up. in his place and denied the author- ship of the Piggott letters nobody believed him, "and in truth." added Mr. Healy, a "lamer state- ment was never made. But what chance, I ask you, would a burglar have of being believed at the Old Bailey when the British House of Commons would not take the word of one of the greatest statesmen of the century?"

As an indication of the vigour with which the purchasing agents of the belligerents are acting, I may mention an incident which has come to my knowledge. Without being too precise, I may say that in one of the Mediterranean ports an ironclad has been for some time in process of equipment at the orders of one of the south American republics. The process has been subject to many delays, the owners of the vessel showing no special anxiety for its completion. All of a sudden, however, the most urgent orders have been issued to get the ship ready for sea. A well-known firm of scientific in- strument makers in this country have been called upon to execute an order given them some time ago without any f nzgestion of urgency, and they have had to deliver the required instruments by special methods and at a few hours' notice. The demand was so sudden that they were unable to make a full delivery from their own stock, and they had to have recourse to purchase from other firms. I am told that they found this a most difficult matter, and that they had to search London to obtain even an extra naval chronometer. This seems to show that the scientific instrument makers in London, as well as other persons whose business is the pro- vision of naval requisites, have experienced a great accession of business since war became inevitable, and that probably more is going On—as is indeed hinted in some of the telegrams from abroad—in regard to the purchase and outfitting of vessels than 'Luis been generally recognised.

General Wesley Merritt, who is to have the imme- diate command of the United States forces operat- ing in Cuba, was born in the city of New York in June, 1836, He graduated at West Point shortly before the outbreak of the Civil War, and was as- signed to active service in the Dragoons, receiving promotion as lieutenant in May, 1862, and as cap- tain in April, 1862. In the following year he took part in General Sherman's raid upon Richmond. At Gettysburg, one os the most sanguinary battles of the struggle between North and South, he was bre- veted major for gallant and meritorious services. Promotion was rapid in those exciting days, and shortly afterwards he was nominated colonel for gallantry at Yellow Tavern and Howes's Shop— commonplace names to be associated with deeds of valor, but the Yankees are a practical people,and go for the enemy wherever they find him, quite irres- pective of euphonious considerations. General Mer- ritt also won renown at Winchester, a much better sounding name, and one familiar to aspiring reciters in connection with Thomas Buchanan Bead's stir- ring dramatic poem, " Sheridan's Ride." For his services at the battle of Five Forks and during the last desperate campaign of the ilonfederates in Vir- cinia he was made major-general. At the close of t he Civil War he had a taste of Indian fighting,after which he was placed in aid of the United States military academy at West Point. He will now he n a position to give lessons to his former pupils in the practice as well as the theory of military opera- tions.

The Prince of Monaco is having a superb steam yacht built at Birkenhead for the purpose of carry- inc on investigations into the fauna of the deep sea. Ile will not be prevented by the political considera- tions from carrying out his intended cruise this summer, since his appointment as an officer of the Spanish navy is purely honorary and would give the United States no right to capture his vessel on the high seas when engaged in peaceful researches. The Prince is becoming quite a familiar figure in English social life, and he is able to maintain his own in a conversation with the chiefs of the English e cisatific world. It is understood that when a suitable opportunity arises be is intending to make a gift of scientific specimens to one of the chief museums of this country.

Mr. Chamberlain's answer to various questions in Parliament has already in effect pronounced the doom of the hut tax in Sierra Leone. The insurrec- tion to which it has given rise will apparently, upon traditional principles, be suppressed before the abolition, since it is beneath the dignity of a Government to frankly correct a blunder. Mr. Chamberlain himself is not free from responsibility in allowing the tax to be imposed after the influen- tial warnings which were given to the Colonial Office that the unpopularity of the tax would lead to serious trouble, and it is costing the exchequer of the colony a sum equal to many years of the return it was capable of producing. The natives have taken to the very efilectual method of render- ing the police ridiculous by destroying their huts and camping in the open air, and this and the hatred of the tax in Sierra Leone should arrest its extension to the natives of the Gold Coast, where it will probably provoke another inturrection.

-- It is from rather an unexpected quarter that the motion comes for a return of the manner in which the Lord Chancellor has exercised his judicial and legal patronage since he has held the seals of office The comprehensiveness of the return also is one of the wonders about it. Even the relationship of the Lord Chancellor to the recipient of the post is to be stated, and it is to be shown whether the relation- ship is by blood or by marriegs. Now, this return may be for vindication or it may be by way of condemnation. The list will be a long one, as it has been his fortune to have to fill upwards of a score of seats on the bench alone. Some of the persons appointed were sturdy Liberals, and I don't know that in the case of the selection of Liberals for seats in the High Court g tl,- remotest thread of relationship existed betw-en Lord Halsbury and the. In the case of the appointment of Mr. Waddy and Mr. Willis to provincial offices there was certainly none. Mr. Gedge, who moves for the return, and who, like a faithful Tory, sits close behind the Treasury Bench, should have added to The long lists of points on which he wants informa- tion the politics of the various nominees, as with- out that it is manifestly incomplete either for purposes of praise or blime.

Ridley' t; announcement of the inten- tion of the Government to introduce a Habitual Inebriates' Reformatories Bill has been hailed by the United Kingdom Alliance and other sections of the temperance party with considerable satisfaC- tion. Short of abolition of the drink traffic, they say, anything is welcome that tends to diminish the eTils arising from drunkenness. Mr. J. Hilton, the Parliamentary agent of the Alliance, believes that the Government will have the hearty co-operation and assistance of the temperance members of the nous') in their endeavour to pass the bill into law. The one blemish on the measure from the temper- ance point of view is its lack of provisions for deal- tvg with habitual drunkards of the non-criminal class. Something should. be done in the way of I restriction and curative detention, it is urged, for men and women who, while inflicting untold misery and ruin upon their families. do not ,11,_m_ ; selves come criminally within reach of the law; ii,nd lit is probable that the temperance members will make strong efforts to rernedy the bill la respect.

Faint echoes of an "international shindy" at Hong Bong, between bluejackets, reached us says the" Chronicle," some time ago. The courtesy of a Seattle (Washington) correspondent places 1.19 in fuller posses- sion of the facts, from which we gather that there was for some time a battle royal between the contending sailor-men. The trouble began between the English and Russian eailers, and culminated in an alliance betweed Russians. Germans, and French. some 400 strong, who barred the way to an Anglo-American force, numbering some 150. Then, says the account :—The Yankees and Britishers, not half the number of the enemy, advanced to the charge, shoulder to shoulder, some crying " Rail Columbia," ard some " God Save the Queen." They drove like a mighty wedge througt the mass of foreigners. The allied German, French, and Russian forces were soon surrounded, and in the words of an eye-witness, " the small squad of Anglo-Saxons knocked seven bells out of them." The police were powerless to interfere. The officers hurried to shore in launches, but the hostili- ties did not cease till the allied forces cried for quarter.

Mr. Wanamaker, vrho has mffered to raise, pay, and command a regiment for the Unit d States Army, is in some respects an extra-ordinary business man. He was once Post master-Gneral of the Republic, and he now has the largest retail drapery, hosiery, and haberdashery hussineas in the world. In the slackest month of the year he sends out, it is computed. 365,000 parcels, while his annual turnover is 13.000,000d015. Among of her things Mr. Wanarnaker's shop contains a picture gallery. The picture are not for sale but for customers to inspect whilst waiting to make their purchases. From time to time he provides conlerts, organ recitals, costume ex- hibitions, " freake,”and the like, which are open without charPe to his patrons.

Lady Henry Somerset's health is now almost restab- lishvd, though she is forbidden platform work. Lady Henry has installed herself as resident manageress of the Duxhurat Industrial Home for Inebriates, .ohich has worked many cures and has not recorded a single failure. Her next contemplated movement is in the direAion nt a home for children under sentence or remand, so that they may be saved from the moral contamination of the prison or workho Ise.

The Scotch patriots who wax so wrathful at the con- fusion of " Euglish " and " British" ought to look after their own publishers. A " Methsdist Times "reviewer asks very pertineatly why the new dictionary of Messrs. Chambers is entitled an " English dictionary." As it is edited by a Scotsman, and published by a Scots firm. and includes such terms as " birkie," " whummle," " toorn," and " warns," he thinks it ought certainly to have been called a" British dictionary."

The Wuhu correspondent of a Shanghai paper writes : —The VPW German" engineer, who was especially engaged at home for steel-rail making at the Nativang Ironworks, has arrived. He turns out to be an English- man, trained in a Sheffield steelworks, but has been employed in Germany for some years, and he was the best man they could find for the work. Rather a peculiar fact !

On Monday the London and North-Western Company announced that it would adhere strictly to the Workmen's Compensation Act. There is to be no contracting out. of its liability ,and the mutual insurance societies exist- ing among the Company's wor kpeople will consequently come to an end, though they may no doubt be reorga- nizsd on a different basis. We have says the " Manches- ter Guardian," nothing Le say to the Company's decision, but it throws a curious light cn the tactics pursued by the Conservative party rather mire than four years ago, when, with the help of the Lords, they succeeded in destroying Mr. Asquith's Employers Liability Bill. The The chief Tory aNument against that Bill was that be- cause it prohibited contracting out it would destroy such mutual insurance societies as those promoted by the London and North-Western Company. Yet, now that the Tory Government has passed a Bill which does permit contracting out, the Company ferwith termi- nates the existence of the societies for which it was supposed, four years ago, to have so deep a regard. It Seems clear that if Lord Dudley's contracting-Out amend- ment, on which the Lords insisted in the winter of 1893- 4 had been accepted by the Liberal Goversnment it would not necessarily have ensued the continuance of the mutual insurance societies on whose behalf it was understood to be pressed. As interpreted by the recent decision of the London and North-Western CompanV, then, the action of the House of Lords was nothing more nor less than a discredit o ble intrigue, and was not even inspired by consideration for the interests of time email minority of workmen to whom contracting out might seem :advantageous.

The sudden death of Colonel Sir Vivian Majendie de- prives this country of a great authority upon explosives and explosions. At one time it seemed as if it would be necessary for the defence of the community that a small army of inspectors of explosives should be at the dis- posal of the Home Office. Through the activity of the dynamitarda, explosions and rumours of explosions abounded, and infernal machines,genuine and otherwiee, were discovered in large numbers. The hero of the hour was then Colonel Majendie, whose business it was to ex- amine the lambs and other dangerous contrivances which came into the possession of the police. Many stories are told of his coolness and daring, and few more courageous exploits have been performed than his open- ing of an infernal machine, set going by clock work, at , a time when the wheels were working and when it was quite possible that he might be blown to atoms. His functions were not confined to criminal work of this description. Explosions in mines came under his ken, and one of the last duties which he discharged before his death was to appear before the Select Committee which is taking evidence on lamp accidents and tbe means of preventine them. The view which he ex- pressed, that any oil is safe in a safe lamp, caused some surprise and disappointment to those uho are agitating for the exclusion of cheap and fiery American petroleum from this country.

Mr. Frederic Harrison writes to the " Times " has been remarked that the Queen Regent of Spain, ad- dressing the Cortes on the eve of war, spoke in terms of proud defiance that would not misbecomo Isabella of Castile, Charles V., or Philip 11. These sovereigns were her predecessors on the throne of Spain, but not her an- cestors in blood. I have not seen it noticed that the Queen Regent is a descendant of William the Silent, by Charlotte de Bourbon, the ex-Abbess, of the Royal house of France. It is a descendant of William of Nassau who to-day rules Spain, in her fierce grapple with a distant Poevsnion in revolt—a province which she has desolated With fire and sword, till again, an in the agent ear own Elisabeth, it has dr?..wn in the intervention of Anglo- Saxon Protestants. It is the Idold of William the Silent, of our own Elisabeth Stuart, "Queen of Hearts," of Maria Theresa, for whom the flung,.rians swore to die, which now flows in the veins of the S )v,reign around whom Spain is being marshalled to-day to defend the Empire of Philip IL. :—" And thus the whirligig of time brings in his revenger."

The rain that began to fall on Tuesciav 0r64 no,x lere more greatly needed than in East Kent. IT Is statPd that many of the wells in and about Canterbury are dry, and several of the large lakes in the neighbouring parks have fallen as much as ei.lite,in inch-g, which is lower than has ever been known, even in the hottest and driest summers.

' 'peen placed netore you. lima° notning in haste. In cases where your judgment vacillates, I pray von i,ei;,-, —4l .- r', -;,,,, Should your verdict be unfavourable to my client, a life-long injury, beyond any powers of reparation, will be indicted on *an innocent person—as . innocent, gentlemen, of the crime imputed to her is you 4W I. Cannot you imagine the terribleness of being unjustly convicted, and ' of being prison at that time of life when, in the full eigoY- 3, inent of youth and health; the mipd has tr 4 ; strongest craving for libertY ? Think, gentieme 'l, of the long, weary days of loneliness, of separat'' .1 from loved ono, of humiliations and indignities, 1 which prison life entails. Think of all this—and, for God's sake, deliberate with care 011'1 judgment over the flimsyevideoce that has been iaid before yon. It is unnecessary for Inc to forther dilate en the weakness of the evidence which the prosecution has put forward. The whole issue of the case hangs upon the testimony 'of l'tcharcl I\lm.grove. yourselves whose word is most worthy of belief— that of the witness aforesaid, or my client? " ' Sir Edward ceased speaking for a moment ; then added, almost in a whisper: "Gentlemen, you cannot return a verdict of guilty against this honourable, noble-hearted, and talented English girl—l can describe her in no truer • terins—when you realise the paltriness of the evidence brought against her, and the terrible consequences that . must follow an adverse verdict. Gentlemen—my task is over. God grant that in pronouncing your aerdict you may be directed aright." For a moment all eyes were turned towards the accused. All knew that the case was nearing its end, and only for a short space longer could her fate tremble in the balance. As Sir Edward was concluding his address she had been visibly moved, and had glanced towards him several times with an expression of deep grati- tude. But now her studied immobility had once lagain asserted itself,. the marble-like pallor of her face alone revealed her acute anxiety. A few minutes' pause occurred before the Judge commenced his summing up. "It has seldom been my misfortune," he began, in a voice not altogether free from emotion, "to be connected with a more lamentable and pitiable case than this on which you, gentlemen, arc called upon to pronounce a verdict. The accused has hitherto enjoyed a position which has lifted her above the range of temptations incident to pecuniary want. Her status in society and the artistic world was such as thousands might envy. Now she stands before you accused of a crone that—" The Judge stopped abruptly and glanced towards the dock,, where the attention of all had suddenly become centred. The accused had fainted and fallen to the floor, where she lay unconscious. Two policemen hurriedly entered the dock and . raised her; and a medical man, who happened to be in court, came forward and offered his services. Restoratives were at once administered, but without avail. Meanwhile the excitement in court was intense, and expressions of sympathy were heard on all sides. 1 Five minutes passed, then ten, but there was no change in the accused's condition. "Under the circumstances the court must adjourn at once," observed the Judge. Counsel on both sides cordially concurred with this humane suggestion. "Allow me to advise you to have your daughter removed at once from this heated court," observed Sir Edward Masters to Mr. Treherne, who seemed too distressed to know how to act under the cir- cumstances. "Shall I carry her to the carriage? " suggested Eric. "Thank you, but—" Mr. Treherne stopped, and looked interrogatively at the doctor. "It is the best thing to do," replied the latter. "Is there danger ? " whispered Mr. Treherne in a low, tremulous voice- " No. The young lady is suffering from prostra- tion consequent on anxiety. The heat of the weather, too, is partly the cause of her condition. The sooner you get her home the better. See— she is beginning to recover consciousness. I should advise your sending for your regular medical attendant immediately on arriving at home. , Meanwhile, she must be kept as quiet as possible." ' A few minutes afterwards, Eric carried the semi-conscious girl to the carriage. As he passed through the crowd waiting outside, with his burden, a murmur of commiseration was heard. "If she don't ever get well again she'll be luckiest," said a man of the costermonger type. "If she were my gal /'d rather follow 'er to the grave than see 'er mired up with ty crew o' gaol- birds—that I would!"

CHAPTER %XXV After Dennis had assisted in placing Gwendoline in the carriage, he turned to• Mr. Treherne and said: "Don't give up hope. There exists, I believe, strong reasons for believing that in the end Miss Treherne will be aquitted." "Thank you for saying that. I only wish I could share your hopefulness," was the despond- ently-spoken reply-. Dennis watched the carriage drive away, and then jumped into a hansom cab. "Thirteen, Hallington Road—and drive quickly! he called out. There was a triumphant gleam in his eyes as he leaned back and lighted a cigarette. "After all, we may yet be equal to that villain Musgrove," he observed complacently. "Seems to me it's not improbable that it will be a case of a man being caught in his own trap." On arriving at Hallington Road the smallest fraction of time possible was occupied in paying the fare and ringing the hall bell. "Is Mr. Lawton at home ? " Dennis asked in a quick voice, the moment the door was opened. "Yes, sir, and you know your way up to his rooms," replied the landlady, who was decidedly averse to mounting the stairs, and had therefore a habit of hinting that her lodger's friends could find their way up alone. Dennis took the stairs at a .rush, and entered Lawton's sitting-room in a precipitous and un- ceremonious manner that al,tonished the occupant, who was of an easy-going temperament. "Well," he observed, removing his legs from the table and drawing himself into an upright position, without, however, rising. "Have you Come to inform me that my maternal aunt has left me a legacy ? " "No—why ? " "Judging by the rate you came upstairs one would imagine you had some good news to tell a falow." "I have come to get good news out of you." "Good news out of met" repeated the other with a short laugh. "You might as well try to get mushrooms to grow on a cherry tree. I have just been penning a touching statement of my financial difficulties, which I propose forwarding to my paternal aunt Sophia. Real it," he added, pushing a sheet of foolscap towards Dennis, "aid tell me if you don't think it is equal to melting a heart of stone." "I'll read it afterwards if you don't mind. The truth is I have come to learn all the facts you happen to know about that patent lock-clasp which you invented for pocket-books." Lawton uttered a faint groan; then, rising, thrust his hands into his pockets and planted himself against the chimney-piece. The non-success which had attended this invention of his was a sore point with him. "That's quickly told," he answered, bitterly. "I took out the patent last January, and thought that my fortune was made, but find the thing is hang- ing fire, and I pave no money for advertising and pushing it forward." "But if what you state is correct, and the patent was not taken out until January—" "Of course it is correct I " interrupted Lawton. "Don't you think I know what I'm talking about? " "Yes; but look here, old man, there is so much hanging on it that I don't like to make too certain of the matter until you have told me more."

"What hangs on 'it ? " "You have read all about Miss Treherne's trial? " "Yes, and heard a great deal more from Hume." "Well, if what you state re the date of this patent lock-clasp is correct, it will secure her acquittal. So I want you to help us as much as lies in your power, and give us all the information you can." "I will—by Jove I will! I have only spoken Once to Miss Treherne, but what I saw of her I "Admired immensely. I wish, though, that you would explain how information about my patent Can assitt the defence ? " "All right, I will then. One of the witnesses, Richard Musgrove, the fellow who says he cashed the cheque for her, has put in as evidence a small pocket-book with your patent lock-clasp. In this appears an entry respecting the cheque, dated the 15th of July of last year. Now, if we can prove that that pocket-book never existed at that time, the prosecution must fall through." !‘Naturally it. must; and what a big bowl over

div.head: WHEEL OF FATE.
div.p: THE WHEEL OF FATE.
BY MRS. BAGOT lIA.RTE, Author of "Love's Revenge," "Bianca," "The Silver Lining," &c., &c.
CHAPTER XXXIV.

Sir Edward Wasters then rose to address the jury for the defence. He began by stating that he must disagree with his learned friend's state- ment that the case was mystery-enveloped. In his Opinion it was enveloped with a conspiracy—not a mystery. His client, who now .1. 00, ,ccused of breaking the laws of her country, was a rising and talented artist and a member of a wealthy and influential family—one who held honour as the most precious possession on earth. All those attributes to existence which render life supremely enjoyable had been hers before these proceedings were instituted. Now she stood accused of a crime which those who knew her best were abso- lutely certain she had never committed. At the moment when she was supposed to have uttered the forged cheque she had a balance of ninety-eight pounds standing to her credit at Messrs. Harding and Co's bank. There not only existed no motive for the crime, but there existed a thousand motiveq for her not committing it. It was impossible not to trace the hand of an enemy in the evidence which the prosecution had brought—that enemy was the writer of the anonymous letter. Counsel did not propose to deal at length with the evidence of either Thomas Brown or Henry Trent. He believed that both had given their evidence in good faith, although they were mistaken in identifying the accused as the person who had uttered the forged cheque. Both admitted they had noticed the dress worn by the utterer of the cheque more than her features, and there remained no vestige of doubt in counsel's mind that they had founded their belief in the prisoner's identity on that dress, having taken for granted that the wearer of it must be the accused. One had been drawn to notice it because of the quaint artistic Algerian trimming, of which he had frequently seen speci- mens before; the other, Henry Trer.t, had noticed it in connection with matching the colour in kid gloves. It was by no means part of these men's duties to take mental photographs of their customers. When it was remembered that they served hundreds of people every week, their testimony as to the indentity of accused was absolutely worthless. His learned friend had assumed that a similar dress to the one which accused was known to possess could not exist. But he personally felt quite certain that a second dress did exist, and that the possessor of it had no desire to place her. self in communication with the police. The theory, then, that the accused must be the uttered' of the cheque simply because she wore a blue gown trimmed with Algerian braid was one which would not hold water in the eyes of twelve practical Englishmen. Was it likely, counsel asked, that if the accused had wished to cash a forged cheque she would have worn a striking-looking dress —one that could not fail to be recognised again? She would, on the contrary, have tried to pass unnoticed, and have adopted some means of dis- guise. With regard to the statement that she had mentioned her approaching visit to Switzerland to Henry Trent, that was not proof of identity. Did not thousands of English people visit Switzer- land annually? Sir Edward then proceeded. to deal with the evidence of the witness Richard Musgrove. His learned friend had described this man as a business man, yet possessing small business capacity, and with an inexplicable partiality for obliging people who wanted to cash cheques of doubtful value. Here counsel stopped, cleared his throat, and, leaning forward, said to the jury in a clear and emphatic manner: "Gentlemen, I never beheld a man who had liar and villain written more indelibly on his face than this witness. The man is no simpleton—no obliging, sweet-dispositioned mortal—but an unscrupulous, conniving character. It is his evidence which has placed my client in the dock. Without his evidence the prosecutioi could have had no locus standi. When he was communicated with, in consequence of the signa- ture to the cheque being pronounced a forgery, he came forward and gave a detailed account of when and how he had cashed it. He had described the accused's dress, conversation, and other details with marvellous accuracy, linking his evidence together with commendable exactitude." Little by little Sir Edward ?Jesters sifted that evidence. He reminded the jury word by word of the surprising tale which the witness had unfolded. How the accused, a well-known character in London society, had come to him, a perfect stranger, and asked him to cash a cheque, offering as an incentive to mention his name to her uncle, Sir Stewart Bathurst. Was it probable that a young lady in her position would demean herself by so doing? Certainly not. If they agreed with him that this part of the evidence was a fabrica- tion, they would at once arrive at doubting every word which this witness had uttered. After further enlarging on this part of the evidence, and endeavouring to prove that it was well known that Sir Stewart Bathurst had taken a house in the locality where Musgrove lived, Sir Edward pro- ceeded to consider the statements with regard to the entries in the pocket-book. This book, the witness Musgrove had stated, was bought about two years previous. Considering the length of time he had had it in his possession, it had retained its new appearance to a surprising degree; a chance observer would have imagined it had never been used at all. However, into this book the witness stated he had jotted down particulars of cheques which he cashed, doubting that they might be met on presentation at the bank. Twelve keen-witted Englishmen were asked to believe that this man was in the habit of deliberately cashing cheques that might be dishonoured. A more ridiculously improbable tale it had never been his (Sir Edward's) fate to hear stated in the witness-box. Here counsel took up the pocket-book and scrutio nised it closely. He read various extracts, com- mented on them, and then passed the book on to the , jury. -

It was handed back to him closed, and on wishing to refer to it again, he discovered there was a difficulty in reopening it. "Allow sue to open it, suggested Dennis, who was sitting close by. "Thanks," replied Sir Edward with alacrity, handing it to him. There were few things he disliked snore than having the current of his thoughts disturbed by outside matters when addressing the jury. But though 'Vane continued tugging at the clasp, and pressing it with considerable strength for several minutes, there was no result. The book appeared as firmly closed as before he took it in his hands.

"Smash it open!" whispered Eric Hume. "He'll want it in a moment, and he'll be deuceal- angry if you haven't managed to get it open." "I'll open it, then," answered the other in r desperate voice; and taking out his penknife he deliberately wrenched open the clasp. Then he handed the pocket-book to Sir Edward, who, however, quickly passed it back to Erie. Dennis took it up and began toying with it. As he was doing so something struck him as curious in the construction of the clasp, and he at once proceeded to examine it intently. "There's a regular lock to it," he mentally observed, "and it must be a patent—something after the kind of patent Lawton brought out a month or two ago. By Jove! it's— "Solicitor for the prosecution wants that pocket- book," observed Eric Hume at his elbow. "Tell him to wait," was the unceremonious reply. "I want to examine it. It's a patent. I must take the number before it leaves my posses- sion."

Dennis pulled out his note-book, wrote the number down hurriedly, then consulted his watch. "It's past five!" be exclaimed; "what an infernal pity! Yes, you can take the clasp now," he added, speaking to Eric. Meanwhile Sir Edward bad adopted a slower and more emphatic style of addressing the jury. The latter were listening with rapt attention. "In a few minutes my responsibilities in this case will be over," he said; "but I cannot resign those responsibilities without impressing deeply on Tet- the far-stretching consequences of your verdica. If it be favourable to my olient—and God gran* thet it may be—then the character of an honour- able and brilliantly clever Englishwoman will be cleared from one of the most cruel and unfounded

accusations, that it 1;;;;I;;;;;-nii misfortune to hear brought against an innocent person. it is no light duty that has been imposed on you by your fellow- countrymen, and I am sure it will not be lightly or thoughtlessly performed. The power _to mar from now until eternity a life that but a short time ago was full of promise, has been pl:‘,c,!din your hands. It is a serious matter—a terribly serious matter for all concerned. I implore you to weigh with care and deliberation every tittle of evidei'ce which has
it will be for Mu,grove It will squash his evidence to smithereens! " .
"He has been the prosecution's trump card, so to ' speak. Had it not tom for his evidence the prose- cution would :lot ho 1-wen ndertaken."

"I thought the case was nearly over." "so. it ig. But any evidence of weight can be put forward en now." ",It will drop 'upon 7,1u5.-;rove as a sharp surprise. I hope be in court wilen the matter is brought for*ard, : His face will 4, a study in surprises." ,"BuktO keep to the pint; if you are positively certain 4.lbutrliWT.We,,. we may as well look up Eric llNtpae9, once, lII' the matter before him, and dthatie ways and means of putting it in as evidence early to-morrow." "Just so. I'm ready row."
"Very well, then. We -,vli drive direct to Queen Anne's Gets, ask how INliss Treherne is, and find out if Hume is :still there." •

Welcome. news awaiti.d thi‘m at Queen Anne's Gate. Gwendoline WZIS stated to be better. As Eric had left the house, they drove on to his chambers and found him lying at fall length on the sofa, looking, as Dennis told him later, "as hopelessly dead-beaten as a man could look." . .
"I my, old man," observed Dennis in a rousing voice, "we have got a clue." "A chue—a clue to what? " repl:cd Eric. "To proving Miss Treherne's innocence( " was the answer. .
"The dickens, you have! Tell me what it is,

sharp! " "Those entries tu that pocket-book are fabrica- tions from beginning to end!" "But have not I said that a thousand times already? There is no clue in that! We cannot prove it." There was a disappointed ring in his voice. _ .

• "We can, though! Didn't you notice that there was a patent lock-clasp to that pocket-book?" "No; I only noticed that it wouldn't open when we wanted it to, and that old Masters looked ready to storm away like fun in consequence." "Lawton knows all about the granting of that patent, and he says that the patent was only granted last January. If so, you have .;onclusive proof that Musgrove bought that pocket-book this year, and that—" "Why, if that's the case, it's—it's as clear as noonday that you have got a clue—a rattling good clue !" cried Eric, sitting bolt upright; and taking up his pipe he began loading it in haste. "Pass me a match, old man," he added, turning to Lawton. "I must have a smoke. It is the only thing to be done under the circumstances. I say, Vane, you're a cute fellow! To think of a man scenting evidence in a patent clasp! Whatever put the idea into your head? " "It was Lawton, indirectly, who made me think of it."

"If good comes of it, you will both win Mr. Treherne's everlasting gratitude. Now, let us discuss what had better be done. What immediate course would you suggest, Vane? " "This is what I should suggest being done," he answered in a slow, deliberate manner. "One of us—for example, myself—having breakfast very early to-morrow morning and getting to the Patent Office the moment it opens, and feeing the 3fficial heavily to look up the date at once. Then taking to court the said official, prepared of course to give evidence and armed with necessary docu- ments. You, Hume, had better be early at court and explain the new phase of the case to Masters." Then, turning to Lawton, he continued: "Be sure to be in court when it opens. Masters will probably put you in the witness-box. I hope you have your letters patent handy; also the blue-book with full specifications of the patent. They will l.e wanted."

"Yes; I have them at toy rooms. By Jingo! what an advertisement this means for my patent!" "It strikes me," observed Eric, thoughtfully, "that nothing could have been more opportune than Gwendoline fainting at that particular moment. I believe it will prove to be a most fortunate circumstance." "So do I," remarked Dennis. "We called at Queen Anne's Gate on our way here, and I was glad to hear that she was better." "She recovered consciousness as we were driving home, but looked dreadfully ill as she was being carried upstairs. To-morrow's verdict means life or death to her—that's my opinion."

div.head: CHAPTER XXXVI.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXVI.

Mrs. Treherne sat near the window in her OWTh room, fanning herself vigorously, and at the same- time lavishing the deepest pity not only on herself and her husband and children, but on her ancestors- and descendants generally. She had just watched the carriage containing Mr. Treherne and Gwendoline drive away, and was now earnestly persuading herself that she would' never see the latter again, "But we shall meet again in Heaven," she murmured with a sob.

"Oh, mum, don't despair so much," said White, the ladies' maid, who had accompanied the family to Les Avants' in a made-to-order voice of pity.. "There's no knowing yet how the trial may end. No one can believe Miss Gwendoline is guilty." "You are right, White; no one could imagire such a thing for a moment. It would be too cruel. She has always been so much beloved, and a great favourite with everyone. But your master told me last night that he is absolutely certain the prosecution would not have been undertaken if that dreadful man, Musgrove, had not given such un- truthful evidence. It is sad to think how wicked some people are! " "Yes, mum, it is. I don't know what the world is coming to, there's so much wickedness and deceit going about! " said. White, as she care- fully folded up some lace. "There is someone knocking at this door, White. See who it is. If it is to say that someone has called, say I'm not at home to anyone to-day. I really do not feel equal to talking. Oh! it is only a note. But even the arrival of a note makes me feel quite nervous. lam so overstrung." "You have been sadly tried lately, mum," replied White, handing the letter to her mistress, and then continuing to fold the lace, but with diminished precision. She was distracted from her occupation by a sudden desire to know the' contents of the letter. _ _
"Oh, White, run quickly and fetch Miss Constance I" exclaimed Mrs. Treherne. "I have received such good news. I can scarcely believe it is true t

_ "About Miss Gwendoline, I hope, mum." "Yes—the real criminal who uttered the cheque has been traced—at least, nearly so. But fetch Miss Constance. I must tell her the news at once I" "I always knew it would come right!'" joyously surmised Mrs. Treherne as White left the room. , "If I co:mid only have induced the others to look upon matters calmly, and to believe all would end well, how much trouble would have been saved But I suppose it was only natural they should be anxious and give way. Poor, dear Henry! How greatly he has aged lately. It is very sad. I do, wish that people would cultivate more equitable dispositions. Not that dear Gwendoline could have been braver; but she always was a good, conscientious girl—wonderfully like me in disposi- tion." Mrs. Treherne smiled complacently, and glanced towards the door. Her yearning to impart the glad news to Constance was momentarily increasing. "Oh, Constance, Gwendoline is saved!" she exclaimed, as the latter entered hurriedly ; "so, at least, we may presume from this letter. Do read it! It is from Eric—good, kind, thoughtful Eric! An important clue has been found which entirely disproves Musgrove's evidence! " Constance read the letter with rising colour, well knowing that Erie would not have penned the few words of hope it contained, without being quite- certain there was a great chance of Gwendoline being acquitted. . .

AFY Mri Trefi-erne and Gwendoline entered the court Eric came at once towards them. There was an element of alertness in his manner which they had not noticed before during the two days' trial. "Did you get my letter before you left? " he inquired at once, speaking to Mr. Treherne. "No."
"Then it must have been delivered a moment or co afterwards. It was addressed to you or Mrs. Treherne, so I e4peet that she would open it." "What was it about? "

--„.— In as few words as possible Eric explained the more hopeful aspect of the defence. "We may win yet," he said, with an encouraging glance in Gwendoline's direction. With these words ringing in ILICT ears she once inure entered the dock.

The Judge --glanced at her as he took his seat, and was surprised to notice her demeanour was lees downcast than on the previous day. Another person also noticed it, and a look of alarm, over- spread his face. This person was Richard Musgrove. _ _
Counsel for the defence immedia*.ely rose and said:
"111 v lord. may I lo allowed to state that somo

facts have Just come to our Rnowled4e which, in my opinion, shews that the testimony of the witness Richard Musgrove is not worthy of el 'moment's credence." "Certainly, you can do so," answered the Judge, knowing that Sir Edward Masters would not have taken this unusual course without adequate reason. "You will remember, my lord." Sir Edward began, "that the witness Richard Musgrove caused a small pocket-book to be put in as evidence. In that small pocket-book entries are to be found dated as far back as eighteen months ago, notably the entry concerning the forged cheque, which hears as date the 15th of July. It has just come to my knowledge that that pocket-book could. not have been in his possession before the beginning of this year. Consequently all those entries bearing dates prior to . that time were written comparatively recently." Counsel then addressed Mr. Vernon, Q. C., and asked that the pocket-book in question should be handed to him, which was accordingly done.

All eyes centred anxiously on the small book. Everyone present knew that a most critical stage in the case had now been reached. "This pocket-book has a patent lock-clasp, you will observe," continued Sir Edward, passing it to the Judge. "The number of the patent is 12578 K, and it was not granted "—here he spoke slowly and with increased emphasis—" until the 3rd of January of this year. The patentee is now in court, prepared to give evidence on this point and to produce his letters patent; also the blue-book, with full specifications of the patent. You will at once see, my lord, that the effect of this evidence will be to prove that Richard Musgrove is a perjured witness, and his evidence a tissue of fabrications. Did he not state in the witness-box that all the details of this forged cheque were entered in the pocket-book by him on the 15th of July? Did he not even put down the hour at which my client called—or, at least, he alleged she called—also the date of the month and the day of the week. You will remember my calling attention to the fact that the two latter did not agree, as the 15th of July fell on a Tuesday last year, not on a Wednesday. From this we may conclude that he consulted an almanack of this year—which was probably more obtainable than one of last year—when he wrote these imaginary details in this pocket-book. "Now, my lord, if a man can commit perjury of the grave character that I have pointed out, is his testimony worthy of one moment's consideration? I will now ask your lordship's permission to call the patentee as a witness." Mr. Vernon, Q. a., at once stated that he would raise no objection to this, and the Judge assented without hesitation.

Edward Hugh Lawton was then duly sworn. He gave the 3rd of January last as the date on which the patent was granted him, and he produced the official blue-book and letters patent to corroborate' his evidence. He further swore that none of the patent lock-clasps were manufactured until after the date mentioned.
As he was leaving the witness-box Dennis Vane, entered the court with an official from the Patent Office. The latter had come prepared to give evidence in support of all that Lawton had just stated.

So conclusively had the latter's evidence proved the date of the patent that it seemed scarcely neces- sary that this official should be called upon to enter the witness-box. However, Sir Edward decided to do so, in order that not &vestige of doubt should be left in the jury's mind, that Musgrove's evidence was entirely unworthy of credence. At the conclusion of his evidence counsel for the• prosecution rose: "My lord," he began, "r have listened with feelings of deer concern to the evidence of the last witness, and I feel it is my duty to state that the facts to which they testify come' on the prosecu- tion as an entire surprise. The evidence of the witness Richard Musgrove is, in our opinion, thoroughly untrustworthy. It will, I know, cause much satisfaction to my clients—and, I may add, it does to myself—that it has been in the power of the defence to bring forward these witnesses, even at this juncture." With these words he resumed his seat.
Mr. Justice Davis then turned towards the jury, and said:

"It is scarcely necessary for me to observe that the facts which ha' o just been placed before the court are of an undoubtable character,, and throw a completely new light on the case. The testimony of the most important witness for the prosecution is now conclusively proved to be utterly untrust- worthy. Periirry of a grave character has been committed. The statements of a witness who coins evidence by making false entries cannot be accepted on any one point. Under the circumstances the interests of justice will be best served by your returning a verdict of Not Guilty. I will add '— here he turned towards Gwendoline—"that I feel great regret for the pain and anxiety that have been inflicted on you." Gwendoline's lips trembled as she inclined bet head in acknowledgment. The next moment the foreman of the jury rose and observed: "My lord, we all heartily concur with what yott have just said, and find a verdict of Not Guilty." A murmur of applause ran through the mirk but was instantly suppressed.
(To , be continued.)

THE EXAMINE, FRIDAY, APRIL 29, 1898.
~ WOMEN'S CHAT."

The Countess Erbach-Schonberg whose name was so frequently mentioned as the Queen's daily companion at Cimiez, is he only sister of the late Prince Henry of I Battenberg. She is the widow of Count Gus' af, and has three sons and sine daughter—the Countess Marie 'Elizabeth Donato- The latter,a handsome bright girl of fifteen, is a great favourite with the Queen, and two years ago paid a visit to Osborne. The Countess, with iser daughtsr has new returned to Schloss Schonberg, the picturesque family seat on the Betgstrasse, which has several times been visited by Her Majesty when staying in Germany. During the early 3 eaes of her widowhood,the Queen's life in Germany was simpler even than at Balmoral. In the summer of 1963 Her Majesty stayed for -tome time at the old mancr house known as the Roeenau, where Prince Albert was born,and the natives had many stories to tell of the unpretentious ways and simple habits of the Queen and her children. The merry, engaging little Princess Beatrice wee the object of much admiration,but coneiderable astonishment was expressed at the strict' discipline exercised over her, and Princelmopold, both being obedient to a word. Princess Helena, the eldest unmarried daughter, was becoming a Allied pianist, and used to be accompauied by Prince Alfred, on his violin, acd the good people at the Rosenau talked long afterwards about their beauti- ful playing. Two things created special astonishment— the tact that the Queeneßoyal Family, and Suite went to church every Sunday, and the constant " tubbing" indulged in by the distinguished party, each having a bath daily: Apropos of baths, it may interest many of my readere to know that sea bathing is a tomparetively modern institution. The.eea was dreaded by the ancients, and Immersion in its waters was looked back upon with a shudder. It was in the middle of the last century during an epidemic of scrofula, that dwellers meth° sea- shore instinctively bathed in the salt water, with so much advantage that a Court physician hearing of it, ordered his patients there by the scores, and seaside hamlets began to grow into towns. Then towards the end of the last and early in this century, Germany, Belgium, andfrance followed suit, and the vittue of sea' bathing became generally acknowledged. The young Queen of ,Holland seems to be thoroughly enjoying her holiday and winning hearts wherever eh* goes. At Imam preparations are in full swing for the coming festivities, and already the shops have put on a coronation Air. ,One .may buy sheets ef portraits on cardboard, deli earthenware, and bandkerchiefiestnoke a Wilheiruina cheroot of Dutch tobacco, eat Wilbelmina sweetmeats, drink out of a coronation tankard, ,play euchre with Wilhelmiva cards, amble on a Wilbelmhaa bicycle, and toast the .Queen in coronation gin. With the shopkeepers of her native country,tbe young Queen undoubtedly immuch more popular thanher mothemithe Queen Regent. The reason probably is that when Queen Wilhelmina sees anything she likes, she orders it to be sent up to the palace without demur,whereas the Queen Regent never fails to ask the prices of things amigo her and often refuses them on the score of their being " too dear." A number especially matched pairs ot plain head and crested canarimehave lately been despatched from Nor- wich to the German Empress, at her request. Norwich is the great. English centre of the canary trade, and one, firm there buys and Bells every year no less than 25,0013 , birds, 20,000.heing norfolk bred. Almost every shoe- maker in Norwich, and a large proportion of the cot. tagers in the country districts of Norfolk, are canary , breeders,the canary being to his breeder, as his pig is to the Irishman " the gintleman that pays the rint. ' In Germany the great nursing for the breeding of canaries is the Hartz Mountains. Many canaries come also from the Black Foresteaut they do not fetch such high prices as the Retie birds, not being conehered such good song- , eters. 'the nightingale and the cuckoo have at length arrived in these Isles of ours for the spring and summer season, and they are now " at home " every day in the woods. In Gilbert White's calendar, the earliest dates upon which the appearance of the principal migrants were noted were—swallow,March 26th ; martin, March 28th; noted were—Swallow,March 26th; martin. March 28th ;1 nightingale April lot; cuckoo, April 7th ; redstart. April 1 Bth ; swift, April"f3th% whitethroat, April 14. In the average year, the middle of April is the arrival time , rthe swallows, and from April 10th to 16th, for the ,cuckos and nightiegetle. Is the nightingale Scotch as well as English? One of the most popular of Scotch naturalists Says it is not. His belief is that the nightingale in Scotland is a tempor- ary absentee" from England, and also Hilt the Eng- lish eird is prominently a cockney. Surrey is the night- ingale's favourite country, and the nightingale region in England extends from the Isle of Wight to Northern Yorkshire. Of course the bird is heard elsewhere, but the forgoing is the best. It appears that the life of the skylark has been a long unblushing sham. " Up with the lark "has always beers synouymous with the earliest of risings, yet if we are to believe an inquiring and industrious ornitholo,gist,the bird in question is a ventable sluggard. The greenfinch, end ttie blackcap will pipe at two in the morning, but the earliest songster to begin the real business of the day is the blackbird. The thrush and the robin are up bee times while the idlest sluga-bed is apparently, the house sparrow. We can forgive the sparrow, for its surrounds i ees are not conducive to early rising, but there is no excuse for the lark. As far back as 1650, levers of nature tried to fix the song of the lark on paper,to write it out in notes to be reproduced by voice or musical instrument. The first cemposer to transcribe the song of the lark was the Je- mit father Athanasius Kircher, auther of the now very rare work lifetsurgia Universdis published in the middle of the 17th century. But the attempt was not entirely successful,or else the lark of olden times did not sing as well as the little bird we know. ' "

By slow degrees the fashions are developing, and we are beginning to see a few adventurous spirits donning spring attire. When the sun shines,as it has been doing occasionally,the wind is generally very cold .but nothing daunted there are many who will wear their new clothes. Nothing will be prettier this year in the Sum- mer sunshine than the lovely organdie muslins.very thin and very clear,with well-covering patterns,some of them appearing to frame the flowers,and always recalling the , days of Lewis XV. and XVI. Another old fashion is coming back to us in the white muslin robes. sold in boxes, richly embroidered with lace let in the skirt all ready to set in the band,and not at all expensive. • Foulard frocks are well to the fore, and delightful specimens the majority are. Foulard was at first jest a , thin navy blue silk patterned by round white spots. ! Then a sprig occurred instead of a spot,next followed a host of varied notions, which, growing gradually more and more daring, reached a climax in the irresponsible and splashed designs of the last two seasons. This spring however,wearied of eye dazz'ing designs,we have placed before us, the simple spot or the sprig of yore. When our grandmothers were young, a partico! small appetite was the order of rii.• day. In fact the sitaher the apt- etite. the more correct it Wonla Was cons.dored. It has been suggested however, that .it- ton chops and other nourishing and substantial • ,as were occasionally devoured in nr;vate, but be thi,r as it may, we have gradually abandoned this absurd, bird- like mode of procedure, and are no longer ashamed to eat a hearty meal in public. The very latest is, that we eat too much! But it should be remembered that cycling, tenni9, golf, rowing, Eic., is rather more hungry work than everlastingly sitting at an embroidery frame, and if any fo;1( feel inclined to dispute the bausiticial resui

n the change, they should attend some large assernhly and take note of the splendid specimens of girlhood and womanhood which are now the rule rather than the ex- ception. The delicate fragile looking girl is at a dis- count, and ths healthy athletic individual reigns in her stead. _ _

Here is the recipe for a delicious pudding. Well grease the bottom of a baking dish, and sprinkle a thick layer of sugar on top. Peel and slice six large apples, and pile on the sugar. Cover, and place in the oven, and bake till the apples are done. Beat the yolks of two eggs, and a small teacup of sugar, till light, then add the whites, beaten to a stiff froth, lastly add a table- spoonful of finely grate bread crunahe, flavor with lemon and pour on the top of the apples. Set the dish back in the oven and cook till the custard is well set. MADGE."

HOUSE CONIVICCEE.

Th. rLERIC stated that he had received a letter from Mrs. E kten who was unable to be present that day, st,i ing that she desired to be placed on the House Com- mittee and one othcr committee. It was dedided that ' he committee should consist of Mrs. Clay,Mrs. Edelsten, It vs. T. R. Matthews, J. 11. Riddette, W. EL drum- mood, Messrs. Billinge, Clarke, Davies, Hibbert, Hick- man, A Jolley, A. J. Jolley, Malkin, Piling, Thornton, and Ashcroft. PADGATE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

This committee is to consist of the following : Rev. W. EL Drummond, Rev. T. R. Matthews, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. FL Thornton, Ashcroft, Ball, Bent, Billing°, Clarke, Davies, Dignum. Hibbert, Houghton, A. Jolley, A. J. Jolley, Knowles, Malkin, and Pilling. THE INFIRMARY COMMITTEE. The Chairman said that it was very important that the members appointeil on this Committee should attend the meetings and givf their attention to the work in connection with the new infirmary. It was decided to re-elect those members present who were on the Com- mittee previously, viz. :—The Rev. J. H. Riddette, Messrs. Clarke, Davies, Halton, Hickman, Houghton, I. Jolley, A. J. Jolley, and J. Pilling. The following were also added; Mrs. Clay. Mrs. Edelsten, Rev. W. EL Drummond, Messrs. Billings and Malkin. THE NEWTON RELIEF COMMITTEE. The Clerk stated that he had received a conomuniea- Mon from Dr. Patterson stating that at the last meeting of the committee a discussion arose as to the advisability of having the Guardian for Burtonwood a member of the conamittee. It was decided to recommend that Burton- wood be included in the Newton district for the purpose of relief.—The Clerk stated that no township which was within four miles of the Workhouse could be put on the Newton Relief Committee. It was therefore impossible for Burtonwood to be included in the Newton Relief District.—Mr. Billinge asked whether they could not petition the Local Government Board for power to do so.—The Clerk said the Local Government Board could not alter the statutory powers which governed relief to the poor.—lt was decided that the Guardians of Newton and Haydock be representatives on the Newt( n Relief Committee. THE ASYLUMS VISITING COMMITTEE.

This committee will be composed of the following members : Rev. T. R. Matthews, Rev. J. H. Riddette, Mrs. Clay,Messrs. Ball, Bent,Billinge, Halton, Hickman, Knowles, Malkin, Dignum, and Hibbert. THE LADIES' VISITING COMMITTEE. The CLERK stated that this committee consisted of Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Edelsten' Mrs. James Fairclough, Mrs. John Fairclough, Mrs. E. A. Fox, Mrs. Joseph Harrison, Mrs. Ycnge, Miss Bessie Dutton,and Miss Massie.—Mrs. Clay said the committee would submit a list of names for the approval of the Board. PROPOSED OFFICERS COMMITTEE.

Mr. A. J. JOT LEY gave notice that at the next meeting he would propose that an officers committee be ap pointed. He suggested that this should be a small com— mittee to whom officers having any application for in- crease of salaries to anake, any complaints to make, sr anything of an official character, could appeal. This bad been adopted in other unions. Tinder the present system in their Union if an officer had anything to say he had to appear before the whole Board. He thought the work of the Unicn might be facilitated by appointing a com- mittee to deal with cases of that kind. The Rev. J. H. RIDDETTE said he would be glad if Mr. Jclley as Chairman of the House Committee would also take the initiative in proposing that a sub-committee be appointed to draw up a scheme of classification of the Workhouse inmates. Mr. amulet; said he did not see how that could be done until the new infirmary was built. Mr. A. JOLLEY thought the matter was one that should primarily come before the Howe Committee. It was a subject which ought to have been dealt with long since. THE DEPUTATIONS TO CONFERENCES, The Cecatemate moved that the Board be represented at the Poor Law Conferences during the ensuing twelve month!. Mr. A. J. jOLLEY seconded, and the resolution was unanimously carried. The CLERIC said at the previous Central Poor Law Conference the Board was represented by Mrs. Clay, the Chairman and the Clerk. Three representatives also attended the North-Western Poor Law Conference. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY suggested that it would be advisable to postpone the election of delegates until nearer the time of the Conference. They could then elect represen- tatives who might be interested in the subjects to be brought forward. The suggestion was agreed to. RESIGNATION OF A NURSE. Nurse Wild wrote resigning her appointment as nurse. Mr. A.J. JOLLEY said it was reported to him that Nurse Wild intended to resign, and be asked the Matron to write to the Secretary of the Nursing Association to see if they had any nurses at liberty. A letter had been received that morning stating that there were none available. He therefore proposed that the Board adver- tise for a qualified nurse with one year's training, salary to commence at £25. The Rev. W. H. Daratmolvn asked whether there was any cause why the nurse had resigned. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said he believed Nurse Wild had not been accustomed to attend patients of the character they had in the Workhouse. He understood that the cmciuct of some of the inmates had been se disgraceful that she declined to stay. It was decided to advertise ter a nurse. OVERSEERS.

- • -- The CLgax said he had received notice of the election a °venoms for all townships in the Union with the ex ception of Great Sankey and Rixton. Mr. HALTOM : I cannot understand why Great Sankey has not been sent in. GIFTS TO THE WORKEIOUSE INMATES. The Master reported the receipt of a parcel of illus- trated papers from Mr. Ashcroft ; primroses from Corn- wall from Miss Monks, Walton ; and a large box of sweets from the Rev. .J. H. Riddette. REAPPOINTMENT OF MR. OWEN. The CHLIRMLN moved that Mr. William Owen be re- appointed as valuer at a salary of £2OO per annum, such remuneration to include all travelling expenses. Mr. Dams:seconded, and the resolution was unanim- ously carried. This concluded the business of the Saard.

.Diet.—Under this head we Will consider what is the best. Every man or woman must be a law unto them- selves as to what to eat, drink, and avoid. The saying 4* One man's meat is another man's poison " is very true, and the time of year, and the climatic surround- ings have much to say in the matter. In the Arctic regions you cau eat and relish fats or fat mixtures such as would be fatal to you in the tropics. Whr do our countrymen suffer sa much from liver complain t? It is because our insular training in the British Isles has induced a lovB for roast beef, spirits and. strong beers, and we indulge in these with one result, liver complaint. Were we only rational and adapted our diet to our enrroundings we would lead healthier, happier lives. Were we to a great extent to shun animal food we would be healthier.

div.head: TRANSLANTIC PIGEON SEUVICE.
div.p: TRANSLANTIC PIGEON SEUVICE.
INTERESTING F2C PE R I MEN TS .

The Paris correspondent of the "Standard " writes : Captain Renaud, of the Compagnie Trans!antique, who on the occasion of his last voyage to New York on the Bretagne, had carried out experiments in pigeon-flying at the request of his company and the Minister of War, bas returned to Paris,and has given in his report. Taken as a whole, the experiments are more satisfaetory than could have been expected. Most of the pigeons released from the ship at sea returned to their houses. or, where carried out of their course by the force of the wind, took refuge on passing vessels. In some cases the birds were thus blown to immense distances, but were ultimately recovered, so that few pigeons were lost altogether. Before the Bretagne sailed from Havre the company notified breeders and fanciers that the birds which returned home should alone be awarded a premium, and as the breeding season has begun only about a huudred carrier pigeons were entered for the experiments and entrusted to Captain Renaud. The following are the main particulars of the report on the interesting event. Four birds were released when the Bretagne was only thirty-two mils from land. They. were all back with their messages within a few hours. It may be remembered that later, while the Bretagne was off the Scilly Island, she fell in with the disabled Bothnia,and rescued her crew of nine,two of whom wan' dead. Seven pigeons were released on that occasion, in spite of the bad weather prevailing. The birds rose to a great height to take their bearings, but unfortunately the gale was too strong for them, and they were seen to cease flying,and allowed themselves to be carried away on their outstretched but motionless wings. One of the birds alighted the next day on a collier in the Bay of Biscay, some three hundred and twelve miles off, thus fulfilling its mission of bringing the news of the accident to the Bothnia. None of the other six birds have been beard of. The weather being still very bad,and the en- treaties of the fair passengers of the Bretagne exceed- ingly urgent, no other birds were sent up until the 'Ves- sel was about half way across the Atlantic. As it had been agreed that the best bird should be sent up from that point, when tli9 moment came Captain Renaud had it brought Co him. Ouce more the ladies pleaded hard, but in vain, and the matter was compromised by allowing one of their number, a young American lady, to set the bird free. Contrary to expectation, it flew direct to America, where it was picked up at a spot about eighty miles from New York. On the return voyage the Bretagnetoak away from New York a batch of about fifty birds, which were released one, two, and three days out. Of these the company hay..i no news. The birds remaining in hand were treed while the vessel was 250 miles, 187 miles, and 125 miles respectively from Havre. Most of these were back in Elavre or Rouen the same day, the riimainder the next or following days. The exact date and time taken are not known, as the owners of the birds had taken no measures to verify the times their birds got back to their cotes. The main point, however, is that none were lost. As this first trial has been so far eatfsfac• tory,the experiments are to be continued,and great care is to be exercised in the selection of the birds, so that a regular and reliable stirvice may be established on the steamers in the interest of the passengers chiefly. In all cases three of the best birds, well-known as long-distance flyors,will be retained for cases of emergency. It appears that birds found with a full stomach on their return are pitilessly sacrificed, as it is a clear proof they have stopped on their way to feed, and thus run the risk of attack by a bird of prey. Indeed, the fact occurred with one of the birds Irons the Bintagne,whicll. carried a.ines- sage from a lady passenger. Oa reaching land it bad rested, and thus gave a chance to a sparrow-hawk,which struck it on the head. MO pigeon managed to. escape, however, but the message reached its destination, four days after the arrival of the Bretagne.

div.head: ELECTION OF' CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF' CHAIRMAN.

The CLERK after a passing reference to his long con- nection with the Board,called upon the members to elect a chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. W. HOUGHTON in rising to propose a Chairman said he was the lather of the Board,and there was not a single member present who was on the Board when he was first elected. He did not claim a special plivilege beyond any other member on that account, but be should feel it a pleasure to initiate the businesst of the new Board by proposing Mr. George Pilling's re-election as chairman for the ensuing year. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Pilling possessed a wonderful capacity for dealing with the work of the Board and f,r conducting its busineis, and he was sure Mr. Pilling's election would satisfy everybody at the end of the year. . .

M. BILLINGE said he had pleasure in seconding the resolution that had been so ably proposed by Mr. Houghton. As Poor Law Guardians they wyre creatures of circumstances. He was not in favour,personally,of any " one gentleman or set of gentlemen monopolizing all the ' offices of a public board. They were, however, in a big tide,and it was not advisable to "swop " horses while they were crossing the stream. Mr. Piiling had acted as a representative to visit London in connection with the carrying out of the important arrangements for the building of the Infirmary, and they felt that at this juncture they could not spare his services for another year. He was delighted to know that the Fairfield Ward in returning Mr. Pilling by such a large maj irity did honour to themselves. He hoped his election to the chairmanship would be unanimous. Mr. S. DAVIES said he had intended to propose Mr. Pilling,and it was his pleasure now to cerdially support his nomination. That there were other old members looking forward to having this position there was not a shadow of a doubt, and he thought it was only fair to give them a chance. Under other circumstances he knew to whom be should give his vote. Hut he thought as there acre six oe seven new members the present chairman and the vice-chairmen should retain office for another ye 4 r. Mr. HICKMAN said he had great pleasure in supporting the motion. Mr. ASICROTT said as one of the new members, he heartily supported the motion. He be ieved there was no gentleman in the room who had given more time to the duties of the chairmanship than Mr. Pilling bad done. The motion was then carried unanimously. Mr. PILLING then took the chair amid applause. He expressed his sincere thanks for the confidence reposed in him. He only hoped that at the end of the year he would be abie to leave the chair with the same feeling of confidence Manifested regarding him, and that tuey would find they hal not made a mistake. THE VICE•CHAIRAIEN.—MR KNOWLES REJECTED

The Rev. J. H. RIDDISTTS proposed that Mr. A. J. Jolley be the senior vice-chairman for the ensuing year. Those who had the pleasure of being associated with him would, he was sure, have felt that he highly deserved any honour which it was in the power of the Board to confer upon him. He did not know whether Mr. Jolley took the record for attendance, but if he was ant ab- solutely first he must occupy the second position. He (Mr. Riddette) had beea struck with the grip which Mr. Jolley had of poor-law work,and the unflagging interest and great devotion of time which be hal shown daring the time that he had been a member of the Board, With regard to the office of vice-chairman, he apprehended that with such an excellent chairman as Mr. Pilling the duties would be very light, but if it happened that Mr. Pilling had oc -asionally to vacate the chair, they could not have a more capable man and a more impartial chairman than Mr. A. J. Jolley. Mrs. CLAY seconded, and Mr. BENT supported the motion. Mr. W. Mr. McLaren supnorted the election of Mr. Jolley. He lived near to the Union's institutions, and had plenty of time on his hands. Further be was deeply interested and experienced in the work of the School Attendance Committee and the Padgate Schools Committee. He had been chairman of the House Committee, and took a great interest in the building of the new Inermary.With reference to Mr. Knowles they knew that he lived some I distance away, and his legal duties occupied much of his time. He (Mr. Hickm in) thought the time had come when the Board should do honour to a man who had been el very much devoted to the work c mnected with it. (Hear. hem) Mr. S. DAVIES said he had great reluctance in votiag over the head of the past senior vice-chairman but con- sidering the work of Mr. Jolley to the Beard he must give his vote in Mr. Jolley's favour. Mr. BILLINGS supported the amendment, and referred to the fact that Mr. Knowles wee absent. div.head: – THE MANUFACTURE OF IRON WIRE
div.p: - THE MANUFACTURE OF IRON WIRE
A QUESTION OF QUALITY.

--- The hearing of the action Bettt v. Herdieckeskoff' which involved the question of the quality of a certain brand of Swedish rod iron whicn had been supplied to various Lancashire and Yorkshire firms. was concluded before Mr. Justice Mathew in the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice on Tuesday morning. De- fendant admitted plaintiff's claim far rod iron supplied, but counterclaimed in respect of a considerable quantity which he alleged seas defective.—The evidence having been heard,and council on Nth'sr side having addressed the court. Mr. Justice lidlthew, giving judgment, said this was a very eeraordinary ease. He did not recollect in his experience ooe exactly like it. The claim of plain- tiffa was admitted,and the dispute between the partice I rested on the ceunter-c"°'. .The case was that the de- fendant ordered certain Swedish iron rods of the plain. life, and having obtained. them, he supplied them to Messrs.Rylands Brothers,Limited,of Warriagton. Messrs. Royston, Son, add Co., and Messrs. J. and A. Binns, of Halifax. It was said that the rods supplied were not equal in quality to what bad been contracted for, and that defendant was entitled to recover damages from the plaintiffs tor the breach of their contract with him. But the first extraordinary circumstance was that the defendant wholly failed to show that he had sustained any pecuniary damage, because, although he made this demand for dainages,it appeared that he had been Paid in full by the representatives of the three firms. without any deduction and without any allowance. The plaintiffs pointed this out as a most significant circuit- etance. How was it possible for a man of business to eay,after he had been paid in full for the particular goods, that he had sustained damage ? The matter re- mained wholly withote. explanation. Mr. Morris, of Messrs. Rylands Brothers, had represented to him that the reason why they had made no claim in respect of the iron rods was that it probably would have to be enforced insuperable objection litigation, and Messrs. Rylande had an objection to litieation, and therefore had paid in full. Although Mr. Morris had given evidence against the quality of the iron,he had been unable to lay Wore the court any evidence whatever of aPowance made to the customers'of Messrs. Rylands to whom wire Made from the iron rAs had been delivered. That wag an extraor- dinary and significant fact. But what was still mere surprising was that Mr. Morris went into the witness- box to prove that the In•Ft on the brand delivered to his cm had amounted to £350. He was confronted with his own letters that he wrote at the time,atid the utmost 'he could say was that £1 a ton was the extent of the damage be the breach of contract. How could he act on his evidence? He was compelled to discard it, and take against it the significant fact that the wire made from the rods bad been supplied to the customers of Messrs. Rylands without any allowance being made in respect of it. One would have expected that with a loss of £350, as in the case of Messrs. Rylande, there would be an immediate rejection of the rods. They were wholly unable to give any evidence that any of the rods were Properly rejected. With reference to Messrs. Royston and Messrs. Binns,of Halifax,the same observa- tion had to be applied. There was no evidence to show that the whole of the rods were not disposed of at a pries entirely remunerative to the several firms. Rig judgment most be for the plaintiffs (Messrs. L.G. Bratt and Co.) on the claim with costs, and on the counter- claim without cost,.
