Tile United States and Spain ; The War, have now been at war for a week, but there has been less fighting and bloodshed than was at first 'expected In fact,, this contest between the two nations bids fair to be one of the reed pacific on record. As it happens the two belligerent countries.. are very unfavourably situ- ated in regard to each other for bringing matters to a crisis., Neither of them is in a position to inflict what might be termed a decisive blow.upon the other. The resources, active or latent, of the States-are enormous enough in all conscience,but they cannot under any conceivable circumstance be brought to bear directly upon the seat of Spanish government, which is, so to speak, the vital part of the Spanish empire. When Nance and Germany went to war in 1870 i it was known that the country which gained the upper hand in the field would be able to dictate the terms of peace in the enemy's capital. That campaign was, therefore, as probably all similar campaigns in modern days, will be, short, sharp, and decisive. France was overwhelmed on the-field of battle and lay prostrate under the heel ofithe German soldier. 'BLit the present dispute can not be settled in any such summary fashion. An invasion of Spain by America is oat of the question. The Americans have not yet won an unchallenged supremacy at !sea, but even, if they had that the transport across the Atlantic of a force sufficient to cope with the Spaniards an their own soil would tax.the resources, of the greatest maritime empire that ever existelj; and the:United States can, by no means lay claim to that distinction. On the other hands Spanish invasion, of the States is unthinkable. In former. centuries the Spaniards under the leadership of. Cortes and Pizarro and other more or less reput-- able adventurers invaded and conquered some of the central and southern parts of the American, Continent, but the present-day inhabitants of, the United States are of a vastly different type from the superstitious Aztecs of Mexico and the mild Ineas4of Peru. And,, besides, when Spain did her great work of colonisation she was the greatest.. or, at all events, the most pretentious of European, nations, while now she is in a condition of rapid decline. There has been an extraordinary transr- ference of power since the days when the. Castilian monarchy drew enormous tributes from, its trans-. Atlantic possessions. The Now Worlt, has in the words of a famous British statesman„ risen, to redress the balance of the Old, Wisan therefore the relative positions Of the two. countriea are taken into account, it is seen that the warfare must almost of necessity be carried on in a slow and probably an unsensational fashion. It has been taken for grantecl in some quarters that Spanish war-vessels will bombard, or attempt to bombard, some of the least protected cities on the American coast-line, but feats of that kind may not be very easily or safely performed, and in any case they would have little or no effect upon the final issue of the struggle. The operations of modern war-ships are strictly limited by the supplies of coal, and the Spaniards aro heavily handicapped in that respect on the other side of the Atlantic, just as the Americans aro on this The vessel whieh ventured upon a bombardment might find itself intercepted by hostile cruisers at a time when, owing to the emptiness of its coal- bunkers, it would have to fight or fly with every disadvantage on its side. Therefore, those bombardments which were to provide such spicy news for the evening papers may, after all

be few and far between. On their part the United States are conducting their warlike opera- tions in a leisurely and caut;ons way, Their fleet is closely blockading Havana, the capital of Cuba, and part of the coast, The waiting policy is perhaps the best under the circumstances, though it hat been varied somewhat by the bombardment of lViatanzaa. Nothing important in the way of ejecting the lipaniards from Cuba can be done until an army of invasion has been gathered together on the and the work of concentrating troops is not being carried through at a break-neck speed. The American army when it is organised will be composed, for the most part, of volun-- tears. Recruits are offering themselves in large numbers in all the centres of population, and it is - wren said that a regiment has been enrolled com-- posed entirely of New York tramps. It is hinted' that the prospect of clean uniforms and free board' and lodgings for an indefinite period cause& much. enthuaiasm in the lower parts of New VOA.: The enrolment of volunteers is, however, only the first andsimplest of the processes that have to be' gone through befcre anything that is worth, the name of ma army can be put in the field. There • is the work of organising and equipping to ' follow, and tkis is, it appears, • getting done very Slowly. There are already, says a correspcs-- dent, more regiments in e-Astonce than the Government can properly train or arm with modern riflesabefore neat autumn. These reports - do not, to say the least, encourage the hope of an parly liberation .of Chiba. Et the same time,delar" ),ells in favour, of the -United States. Spain is ' 'ready beginning to find it extremely difficult to ,*se the money necessary to carry on the war, and it is not at all improbable that okte‘• may even be "starved out" of CUba by 3- process of sheer financial exhaustion.

THOUGH the prevalent foaling in this • 1 country,in connection wi'..l; the war ICroucip i ta is undoubtedly on the American side,. there is in some circtes a good deal of sympathy- with Spain. That country has, howeve74 brought these troubles upon herself by hot wretched and inhuman misgovernment of the ill-fated 'Cubans. Mr. G. C.MUSGRAVE,WhO acted as a newspaper cor- respondent in Cuba, gives some shocking details of the methods adopted by Spanish generals in their unsuccessful efforts to put down the re- bellion. General WRYIEU was described as the " butcher" in America and he appears to have deserved that title fully as much as the-Serum' - deserved that of "the assassin." Wirana was sent to Cuba to suppress the revolt, and he seems to have made up his mind to suppress it by ex- terminating the Cubans whether they carried arms or not. He issued an order • that all the rural population of Western Cuba, must within seven days come into the different fortified places held by the Spaniards. By this order thousands of people—men, women and children--who had continued at work on their farms and p.lantations were taken from their homes and means of liven- - hood • and concentrated on pieces-of ground which ware fenced off, by barbed wire. If they ventured beyond these fences they were liable •to be shot down, and yet they RODO-not provided with food by the inhuman dictator. Some of them • had small amounts of money with which they purchased a few. neces- saries, but, generally speaking,the poor people died by thousands of starvation. Mr.Musor.A.vn visited • one of 'these settlements on two occasions. On the•first occasion there were some thousands of human beings in it; on the second there were . about- a score of human skeletons. Dying mothers werato be seen trying to suckle dying children at f their breasts. The BiallOP of Havana, himself 3 Spaniard, admitted that three hundred thousand • bodies had been buried in consecrated ground,and ,it is calculated that two hundred thousand other , bodies have been buried elsewhere. The Cuban atrocities appear to have been worse than those of Armenia, and that being so one can only hope that the Spaniards will soon be bundled bag and 'baggage out of the island they have so -dreadfully mi swerned.

One of the most unpleasant features of a Parish Councilnelection is the cost in which it involves the township for enjoyingjhe privilege of choosing representatives front amongst the rival candidates. At the annual parish meeting a poll can be de- • mended by a very small section of the elec- tors, the, cost of which falls as a matter of course upon the whole of the ratepayers. And yet it is a peculiar circumstance that the result of the election at the parish meet- • ing is nearly.always more or lePs altered when the ballot is introduced. The election at Great Sankey may beAaken. as-a case in point. At the parish meeting several of the retiring members of the • Council were defeated, but when an appeal was made to the whole of the parishioners, the return of the ballot pipers showed that the inhabi- tants had such confidence in the retiring. members of tbe Council that they were re-elected without exception. The composition of the Coun- cil is therefore 41,as you were" before the election. with the little difference that the election expenses hare to be paid and these will perhaps moan abota a helfpentiy,in the E on the rates.

A carious coincidence occurred last week George Hilton, father and son of the, came name have been admitted to the infirmary for treatment,. through injuries sustainedin accidents. Both acci- denta.tooa place the same morning at two different places. One with an imaginative mind in these mattere,might say this was.a case in point for those. who, uphold the theory of thoughts and acts "-sympathetic."

No one could contend,, with any show of reason.. that the lot of a clergyman of any denomination iB, synonymous with the term, "a bed of roses,"•-but Mr. Ireland, the vicar of St James' Church,, Hay- dock,appeare to have a particularly harrassing, time. For some years helms had to-view tha approach of the annual vestry meeting, not as the coming of a peacefalpractical, business meeting, but aagather- ing where the fulminations of a year's growth are poured out, by certain members of the congregation., A fortnight ago the annual explosion occurred kvery few minutes after the opening of the meeting,, and the Rev, F. J. Ireland left the chair, declared the meeting closed, and turned the lights aut. Then Mr. Robinson, the peoples' warden, oftiaated as 4 chairman over what was, at least in one respect, a very unenlightened assembly, until the cover of darkness put an end to the proceedings. Last week the wardens called another meeting, found the church doors locked and calmly proceeded with the business in the open air, Mr. Robinson presiding from his place of vantage on the vestry steps. Apparently Mr. Ire' and has a predilection for ritual w:lich goes against the grain of a number of parishioners who. openlY, declaim against what they consider the illegality 01, the Vicar's practices. Mr. Ireland's high-handea behaviour when" tackled" is not the best course for him to pursue if he has the least, desire fa 6111 e ndurable existence in the future.

THE ANNUAL MEETING.

The first meeting of the newly elected Board was held at the Workhouse,Dutton,on Tuesday afternoon. There were present the Rev. Dr. Gistaldi, Messrs. S. raylor J.P., T. Lea, J. Meadowcroft, and A. R. Norman J.P., S. Yarwood, the members of the Rural District Council, with Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. G. F. Ashton (de- puty clerk).

div.head: NSW CAIRN.

The Clerk was al;P;;ii;ted chairman pro tens. Mr. Wright asked if they had the power of appointing an outsider to the post of Chairman or vice-chairman of the Board. Mr. Ashton • The Act gives you power to elect an outsider to those offices. Mr. Wright said Mr. J. Mosely Williams had been a Guardian for some time, and the members of that Board knew of the noble work performed by him at the time of the smallpox epidemic. In courtesy to him for the work he had done he (Mr. Wright) considered they should elect him chairman of the Board. Mr. Taylor said he was sure that the gentlemen who had sat on that Board for a number of years would agree with him that Mr. Williams was as good and as ardent member as they had on that Board. He was sure that all the old members would be very pleased to see Mr Williams back again. Dr. Gastaldi supported the motion. Admiral Jones-Parry said he was sorry to move an amendment at the first meeting. He proposed that their late chairman be re-elected to the office. Hs had been an excellent chairman Mr. Knowles I have no intention to serve as chair- man again. Admiral Parry : I am afraid you are rather bashful. The chair has been well filled and the chair under your rule has been strong enough to hold you. (Laughter). Mr. Pilling seconded the amendment, and considered it a slight on Mr. Knowles if the motion was not carried. Mr. Woodward supported ths original motion. Mr. Wright said he proposed Mr. Williams. knowing that Mr. Knowles positively declined to act again. Mr. Knowles: I wish to withdraw. Admiral Parry said he did not wish to withdraw his amendment, but as Mr. Knowles would not accept office he reluctantly withdrew it, with the consent of the seconder The proposition was pat to the meeting and carried with acclamation. TILE VICH-CILEIEMAN.

Mr. Woodward moved that Mr. Stokes be the vice- chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Baxter seconded, and Mr. Wright supported, the latter adding that Mr. Stokes had been a guardian for sornetking like 2.0 years. Mr. Yarwood said he proposed ancther gentleman for the simple fact that Mr Stokes did not attend the meet- ' ings so often. 110 Proposed Mr. Norman as the vice- chairman. He considered Runcorn ought to be a little more represented than it had been in the past. Mr. Norman intimated that he had no desire to let his name stand as V.C. Mr. Mclntyre seconded. Mr. Norman thought there were older members to fill the post than him. Mr. Stokes was a much older mem- ber, and seeing he had an hint about his attendances,he perhaps would remedy that. The motion that Mr. Stokes be vice-chairman was

carried. The Clerk then vacated the chair and as Mr. Williams (the chairman) was not present Mr. Stokes took the chair. He thanked them for the honour conferred upon him. He felt unwnrthv of the post. He had been at- tending that Board for 20 years arid during that time he had seen that chair occupied ky men of honour. He had seen the late Canon Barclay in the chair,and he was sec- heeded by their Clerk, Mr. J. Ashton. The latter was eucceeded by others who had been equally worthy, but he (Mr. Stokes) felt quite unworthy to succeed such a noble train that had occupied that chair. With refer- ence to what had been said about his attendance he took it in a kindly spirit.but they ought never to take a thing I without an explanVion. Ile,knowing that Mr. NOM 111 was always on the spot endeavoured to give him (Mr. Norman) a share of the work (Laughter.) He would endeavour to work In harmony with the chairman and the other members of the Board. If the Chairman erould let him know when ho could not attend he (Mr. Stokes) would be willing to make any sacrifice to be present. THE COMMITTERS.

div.head: "A HEAVEN-SENT FOREIGN SECRETARY."
div.p: "A HEAVEN-SENT FOREIGN SECRETARY."

Mr. Roscoe Brunner, speaking on current politics at a public meeting of Liberals of the Widnes Polling District on Thursday night (last week) at Widnes, said criticism of the preeent Government was rather difficult, because they had not done much. They had promised a lot, but very little was being accomplished. The Government came into power with a huge majority, a strong Cabi- net, and a heaven-sent Foreign Secretary. (Laughter.) Coming to foreign affairs, Mr. Brunner referred to China's request for pecuniary help from this country. They required concessions from China in return, but larger concessions were asked for than other nations were disposed to allow them to have, and they were practi- sally between two fires. In the unlucky event of Russia and Germany combining they would And themselves in a dangerous position. we had an agree- meat with France that Zanzibar should not be interfered with, but they had already allowed Germany to get posseuion in the mainland, and having allowed them to Interfere with their agreement with France they could not raise any question when the French required Mada- gascar. They had a csmmercial treaty with Madagais• car, and when this posseasion was annexed by the French in IBM they lest a large trade between India and that place. Lord Salisbury had pro- tested against that, but it was quite evident that nnthing had been done. They had lost the trade in Siam, and we had surrendered a commercial treaty with Tunis. In the Upper bile they had the French endea- vouring to reach Abyssinia before them, although they bad made a geed advance. The battle at Atbara was a signal victory, die very lareoly to the genius of Sir Her- bert Kitchener. (Hear, hear.) They would say of the Government, "The can sit deawn, we have seen thee." Turning to home affairs, there had been considerable doubt as te whether the question of Home Rule was still in the forefront of Liberalism. For his (Mr. Brunner's) part he said it was, and Mr. Morley agreed with him. He would not abandon it. Lord Randolph Cnurchill, speaking at the time the English Local Government Bill was introduced, said that Home Rule should have been granted at the same time. Irishmen did not like the rule of Dublin Castle, and it was not at all likely that they should do. It represented alien rule, and the Irishman never would like alien rule. There should be local government there on the lines of the English Local Government Bill. With respect to the employers' liability question, the Government had left out domestics servants. They bad not included merchant seamen, agricultural labourers, and persons engaged in building operations unless steam was employed. They re- jected the proposal of a Liberal to include all workers. The speaker passed on to the educa- tion question, and characterized the Bill of 1190,that of rating the national expenditure to 2115. per heed and local to 20s.per head,as an iniquitious proposi- tion. This Bill was thrown out last year. Two Bills were breught in last year, one giving money to the Voluntary schools, and the other to necessitions Board schools. It was a good policy to give the Voluntary schools money,but they were treated four times as well as the Board schools. The question of religious teaching in schools was a very difficult one. It was necessary that the children should be taught religious subjects,but it was not fair that any child should be taught by a minister of any religion of which the parents did not ap- prove. (Hear,hear.) In conclusion, Mr. Brunner ex- pressed his adherence to what be turned the good sound Liberal principles and the true socialistic doctrine of v the greatest good to the greatest number. (Applause.)

RUNCORN FREE LIBRA.RY COMMITTEE. 'DEATH OF MR. B. KNITETON, AND MR. Gt. MOSS, OF RUNCORN.
THE FIRST MEETING.

The first meeting of the newly elected Library Corn- mi:tee was held on Tuesday night at the Town Hall, Runcorn, There were present Messrs. D. Bisbrown, W. Handley; M. J. Sweetman, G. H. Kirkham, A. R. Nor- man, R. H. Posnett, T. Riley, W. Hankinson, J. Prit- chard, M. L. Davies, and J. D. Jones, (librarian and secretary). MR. lIISBROWN RR-ELECTED CHAIRMAN. On the motion of Mr. Hankiuson, seconded by Mr. Sweetrnan, Mr. Bisbrown was re-elected chairman. The proposer observed that Mr. Bisbrown bad proved a very efficient chairman during the past year. Mr. Bisbrown in accepting the office said he consi- dered the position was an honourable one to occupy. It had been a great pleasure to him to Preside °vat* their meetings from month to month. They had worked har- moniously together in the past and he hoped they would still continue to do so in the future. The present year would be a very important one. They were looking forward to the opening of tia, new library premises. It was ten years since the last extension, and they would ha delighted to have the impending alterations com- pleted.

The ranks of Runcorn's public men have been consi- derably thinned of late by the band of death. This week it is again our painful duty to record the deaths of two prominentmen of the town, in the persons of Mr. Ben- jamin Kniveton and Mr. Goorce MISS. MR. KNIVETON.

Mr. Ileiveton had been ailing for a considerable time, and his death at the age of 53 years, which took place on Tuesday afternoon at his residence 73, Greenway-road, was not altogether unexpected. He had been attended by Dr. McDougall, who did everything possible to alle- viate the suffering and prolong the life of bis patient,but despite all this, Mr. Kniveton succumbed at the time stated from lung affection. The deceased gentleman came to Runcorn 27 years ago, from Astley, in Lanca- shire, and commenced business in Church-street, as a boot and shoe manufacturer. Shortly afterwards he became the agent to the Astley and Tyldesley coal and salt company, which position he hold up to the time of his death. He was known in that capacity throughout a wide district in Cheshire, and was greatly esteemed by his firm and all those with whom he came in contact. In polities Mr. Kniveton was an ardent Liberal. Shortly before the general election of 1885, he threw himself heartily into political affairs, and became a re- cognised leader of the Liberal Party in the town. As a public speaker on political questions, he bad no rival amongst local men. By his grasp of public questions and his clear way of express- ing his views be commanded the admiration of all who beard him, whether opponents or friends. For several years he acted as registration agent for the Liberal party In the Eddisbury division, and was also the election agent for Mr. Tomkinson, J.P., in 1687, and also for Mr. Roger Bate in the subsequent contest in 1392. His work in that very extensive agricultural diviiion entailed a large amount of public speaking, and his services were in very great request especially in expounding the Local Government measure of 1694. Mr. Temkinson valued hie services very highly. His death will be a distinct 1 i'loss to the Liberal party throughout the district. In 'religion Mr. Kaiveton was a Wesleyan and a prominent member of St. Paul's Chapel, High-st. In connection with the church he had occupied almost every office. He was chapel secretary and had charge of all the property belonging to the Runcorn cireuit. He commenced his career as a local preacher as soon as he came to the town, and almost immediately took rank as one of the most acceptable preachers in the circuit. He frequently occupied the pulpit of St. Paul's Chapel, and his discourses, which were of a high order, were much appreciated. His style though not emotional or theological was marked with strong commonsense and hard-headed reasoning, his object being to make religion appear reasonable and a so much so, that he had been on more than one occasion taken for a regular preacher. During the last few years of his life he had tsh ireegver foren t eavnede yddiagyai us •. His manner in the pulpit was ad to reliaguish pulpit work,but he found equally congenial service in the Men's Bible Class which he instituted in connection with St. Paul's and over which he presided Sunday ylly prepared afternoon tNchdeiaeelrfilvfyeearietnurgreerayof the service. The attached to him and frequently untilafmnduedme address debbs shsi wsmwhl were at te i wlhil ineasees ps the se bore testimony to the good that he accomplished. The light he threw on passages of Scripture was intensely interesting and useful, and the members had shown their appreciation of his services by presenting hint with gifts. The public generally will receive the ietelligence of his death with the deepest regret. He leaved a widow, two sous, and three daughters to whore,we are sure the pub- lic will extend the fullest sympathy in their sad be- reavement. The funeral takes place this afternoon (Friday) at the Runcorn Cemetery. MR. MOSS.

REFERENCE BY THE VICAR.

Reference was made to the late Mr. J. E. Langshaw by the Vicar (the Rev. Canan Wood) in his sermon at the Parish Church on Sunday morning. Taking his text from the Epistle of St. toter chap. 2, • 21, the rev. t preacher said the lot of e Christian was suffering and his duty s. patience. Within the last few days they had lost on of the members of that congregation, very well-know, to them all. Just a week ago that day, James L sngshaw passed away from them. He was one whom he had known almost since he came to Runcorn. Deceased was a member of his (the preacher's) confir- mation class and was confirmed in that church a little more than ten years ago. Since that time he had,he be- lieved, been a most faithful member of that church and congregation and a regular communicant. He interested himself in the work of the church and was a long time a member of his Bible class. He was also a ringer and a Sunday school teacher, and an elected officer of the church. He was a man of a very kindly disposition, a man ef sense and intelligence, and a useful niters, as he beard him truly called. He was a man who took part in other public things,and they saw on Wednesday how highly he was esteemed net only by the members Of that congregation but one might say by the whole town of Runcorn. Be had left them a good example. He was taken away before he bad reached the prime of life,and from his dear ones at home. His removal from the place where he was so well-known was not without a direct purpose they might be sure. They all knew that as he went he was not afraid to go, and they fully be- lieved he west with Christ. That as he had endea- voured to live with Christ so with Christ he died. There were certain people, it did not matter what their religious opinions might be, who appeared to c ccupy life with the greatest amount of comfort that they pos- sibly could secure, and cared nothing whatever for the sorrows and trials of other people. They saw this in the matter of hospitals. There were thousands who paid no attention whatever to these important institu- tions. They seemed as though they were separated by some barrier from their fellow human creatures, and would neither help nor take an interest in them. It seemed to him that there was something of the same kind in religion. That was to say,that people who were religious in a sense, and attended the services and liked them to be well conducted, and who were interested in social things connected with the church, and were more or less distinguished as church people, had somehow or other not got a real vital interest in Jesus Christ. All religion without Him was noaght, and he could not help thinking that God took away one and then another with a direct object and purpose. In conclu,ion, the rev. preacher said he did not want in any way to attempt to terrify or frighten,or to say too much of the uncertainty of life, a fact which they all knew very well. He did want them not to miss those lessons which God had sant to them. During the service the hymns " Fight the good fight."" On the resurrection morning,' and" God of the living, in whose eyes," were sung by the choir and congregation, and at the close Mr. J. Johnson (or- ganist), played the Dead March in "Saul," the congrega- tion meanwhile standing.

DEATH AND FUNDRAL Or Ms. SAMUEL DUNN. On Saturday at the Warrington Cemetery the grave closed over the remains of Dim Samuel Dunn, wife of Mr. Dunn, of Park, near Sheffield, formerly of Warrington, and daughter of the late Mr. Isaac Hayward, of this town. The deceased lady was well-known in'Wesleyan circles, and prior to her removal to Park four years ago she was identified with Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel and Silver-sc. schools. :the was only 32 years of age, and her death came as a painful surprise to many friends. She had been in failing health since Christmas, and died on Thursday last week. The remains were conveyed by train on Satur,,ay and arrived at War- rington at 2.26, and were thence conveyed to the Warrington Cemetery. The bearers were Messrs. Joseph Owen, T. Brans, Charles Allen, E. White- house, Joseph Bailey, and Walter Jennings. Amongst the relatives present were :—Mr. Samuel Dunn (husband), Mr. Stanley Dunn (son), Mr. J. W. Hayward, J.P., Mr. Isaac Hayward, Mr. Andrew HaywardlsAhlfrb e ( Dunn, 431 a (Glasgow), brothers; Mr. William Dunn, Mr. r. William Isaac, arid Mr. A. thers-in-law). S-veral friends also wit- nessed the last rites as a mark of respect. The Rev. G. Harbottle was the officiating minister, A large number of floral tributes had been sent. At Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday morning the organist, Mr. Wadsworth, played " The Dead March" in" Saul "at the close of the service, dur- ing which the congregation stood.

div.head: BANKRUPTCY OF MESSRS. T. AND W. CROSS. THE JUDGE REFUSES TO DISCHARGE THEM. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, Messrs. Thomas and Walter Cress, whe formerly carried on business as buildereat Warrington applied;through Mr. Arthur Brobelpe)for their discharge as bankrupts. The application was opposed by the Official Re-
div.p: THE BANKRUPTCY OF MESSRS. T. AND W. CROSS. THE JUDGE REFUSES TO DISCHARGE THEM. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday be- fore his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, Messrs. Thomas and Walter Cress, whe formerly carried on business as buildereat Warrington applied;through Mr. Arthur Brobelpe)for their discharge as bankrupts. The application was opposed by the Official Re-

Mr. C. J. Dibb, official receiver, Manchester, read a report, describing the career of the bankrupts, to show cause why their application should not be acceded to. It stated that the bankrupts filed their petition on the 7th October,lB96 The liabilities were estimated at £1,897 10s. 241., the proofs actually admitted amounted to £1,822 15s. 91., and the probable claims not admitted amounted to £435 183. 81., making a total of £2,258 2s. Bd. £360 123. 11d., the ditTehnce between actual and probable liabilities, principally arose in respect of the claims of Melsrs. Richard Evans and Ce. and Thomas Smith Burgess,which were understated by £254 123. 3d. and £B9 93. 41. respectively. The as- sets were estimated by the debtors to produce £lO6 03. 21. They actually produced £lO7 173. 91. A first and final dividend of 4.1 in the pound was pail on proofs from £1,822 153. 91. Thomas Cross lascl separate lia- bilities amounting to £lO, but no proofs were lodged azainst his separate estate. The assets realised £3 183., which was absorbed in pay- ment of costs. Walter Cross had neither _

liabilities not assets in respect of his separate estate. The bankrupts commenced business as builders in part- nership, under a verbal arrangement only, in Warring- ton 1891, practically without capital. Each of them admits a prior failure, Thomas Cross in 1888, when he effected a composition of 7s. Bd.of liabilities ender £lOO. contracted as a jobbing bricklayer. Walter Cross in 1886 made a deed of assignment for the benefit of his credi- tors, his liabilities heing about £l2O. He is unable to say what dividend was paid. His liabilities were con- tracted as a jobbing bricklayer. The bankrupts allege that the joint insolvenoy is attributed to overbuilding, want of capital, and law costs. Probably the real causes were speculating jerry building without a capital and failure to keep proper books of account. They appear to have acquired from* various persons upwards of 1,200 square yards of land for long terms of years, to have built a large number of houses therm, and then to have raioed what loans they could thereon and given charges thereon to some of their creditors as security for past indebtedness, not only by first charges, but in some cases by second,third, and fourth charges. How the loans were applied it is impossible to say, there being no books of account, but the unsecured liabilities mainly represent building materials, and it is submitted they were obtained re- gardless of the fact that there was little likelihood of their being paid for and that properties with which they were built were assigned to mortgagees without regard to their liabilities for such materials, and without re- gard to the fact that the equities in the mortgaged pro- perties were not worth a single penny. In fact, the bankrupts admit by their joint statement of affairs that the mortgagees' claims were unsecured to the extent of £778. The bankrupts have not filed the prescribed deficiency accouet. They say it is impossible from our books and papers to prepare a reliable deficiency account. We can only state that the deficiency is accounted for by loss on building, law costs, kc., and as a matter of fact £2,150 43, lli. shown le; this report remains practically unexplained." In conclusion the report gave the followine reasons why the application should not be granted :—" (1) That the bankrupts' assets were net of a value equal to 10).in the L on the amount of their unsecured liabilities and that that has arisen from circumstances for which they must be held responsible ; (2) that the bankrupts omitted to keep:such books of accounts as are usual and proper in the business they carried on and as sufficiently disclosed their business transactions and financial position within three years immediately preceding their bankruptcy ; (3) that the bankrupts continued to trade after knowing themselves to be insolvent, as appears in this report (4) that the bankrupts have been guilty of Misconduct in carrying on business and contracting fresh liabilities prior to the date on which they knew themselves to be insolvent in wilful ignor- ance of the true financial position ; (5), that the bankrupts have contracted the debts provable in their bankruptcy withour having at the time of con- tracting them any reasonable or probable ground of expectation of being able to pay them ; (8), that the bankrupts have failed to account satisfactorily for the deficiency of assets to meet their liabilities ; (7), that the bankrupts have brought on their bankruptcy by rash and hazardous building speculations ; (8), that the bankrupts have within three months preciding the dAte of the receiving order when unable to pay their dcbts as they became due giving undue preference te two of el their creditors, as stated in this report ; (9), that each of the bankrupts has on a previous occasion mode a compositiou or arrangement with his creditors as stated in this report. The bankrupts' conduct during the proceedings under their bankruptcy has been only ntoderately satisfactory, in that both of them have treated their position somewhat flippantly, the bankrupt Walter Cross, too, at times being inclined to be imperti- nent." Mr. Arthur Browne then addreseed the Court in sup- port of the application. He said there was nothing in the Official Receiver's report to .prevent his Honour feom using his discretion and discharging the bank- rupts. He hoped to be able to convince the Court that what was alleged against Messrs. Cross had not been wil- fully done but in ignorance of their true position owing to them not having kept proper hooks of account. That was one of the points brought against tbem by the Official Receiver. It must be remembered that these two ' men were working bricklayers with practically no edu- cation at all. It was all very well for the Official Re- ceiver to say that they ought to have kept proper books;l they all knew that, but that was assuming they had sufficient education to do so. Such mea as the defendants thought that if they kept a hank- ie,' account they Would know perfectly well how they stood. It was owing to bad book-keeping that many of the charges of the Official Receiver arose, such las for instance the charge that they continued to trade ' after knowing themselves to be insolvent, and also that at contracting fresh liabilities when in an insolvent position. He did net suggest that all the charges couli be explained away by bad book-keeping but to some ex- tent they could. The Official Receiver alleged that each of the bankrupts had on a previous accasioa made. composition or arrangement with creditors. With re- gard to Thomas Cross he paid a compeeition of 7a. 61. in the and that was accepted unanimously by the creditors. It did not come before the Court, and the liabilities altogether did not arnouct to £lOO. With re- gard to Walter Cross he had ascertained that els credi- tors in his arrangement with them previous to thel preseat bankruptcy had received 20e. in the £ and the costa from the trustees. Mr. Cross left in the hand.) of a trustee a secerity which had enabled the creditors to receive their money in full. That charge of the Official Receiver therefore fell to the ground. With regard to the statement that Messrs. Cross gave undue preference to two of their credltoro,ho might state that one of the creditors alluded to happened to be as usual the Warrington Slate Company,and the other was the District Bank. Messrs. Cross paid the Warrington Slate Company thousands of pounds for bricks, slates and building materials. The managing director began to press for payment, and as the company was the only Arm from which they could get goods of a certain de- scription which were eeeied, Messrs. Cross consented to give them a second charge on some cottage property. He (Mr. Browne) was told that that second charge would not realise the firm's account in full. With reference to the preference given to the bank, what was a man to do when in difficulty and being pros;erl by creditors? The defendants were oblie,ed tee give secu- rity to the bank or they would have stopped payment. Innocently enough they gave the bank a second mort- gage as detailed in the Official Receiver's report. it was due to him to say that these men came to Warrington to build furnaces for the Pearson and Knowles Coal and brie Company. The furnaces had to be built on Saturday night anu Sunday and they employed men under them. They did the work very well, but they were idlo during the remainder of the week. They were persuaded to build four small cottages and take some land. They were obli ted to pay £lO 103. before they got their lease, and when they went to another firm of solicitors to get. mortgage they had te pay a further sum of ten or 12 guineas in costs. These were the law costs which had been alluded to. It would therefore be seen that on four cottages worth about £BO or £9O apiece there would be law costs of about twenty guineas as Messrs. Cross were without capital. There was also the interest on the loan to be paid,ranging from four to five per cent. That was how they began. They were persuaded to go a step further, and helped on by builders' firms and solici- tors they continued building until the coal strike of 1894. At that time they had 154 houses in occupa- tion, and they could imagine what effect the strike would have upon Warrington which de- pended on coal from the Wigan district. The tenants were liable to pay their rent and Messrs. Cross lost a considerable amount of money, whilst at the same time they had to continue paying the interest on the mortgages.Travellers induced Messrs. Cross to go on building, and some of the firms had received thousands of pounds for goods supplied, and not one was there that day to oppose the application. The bankrupts took nothing out of the estate for their own living. It was well known that they were expert furnace builders and they got sufficient from this work to keep them respect- able without taking anything out of the business. No one could charge them with having been guilty of drunkenness or gambling or of any extravagance. They even lived in houses which were only rented at Se. a week. All the elements were wanting which would cause his Honour to refuse the order entirely. These men had worked from five in the morning until 8 or 9 o'clock at night. They had wasted no time bat unfortunately it was the same old cry they had kept no books. If they had had books this bankruptcy would never have occurred. They employed an old army pensioner to keep books for them but he

failed to carry out his duty in this respect. ,It was quite true as stated by the Official Receiver that the , bank- rupts had drawn £5,000 from the bank in three years, and that a further sum had been drawn by the pen- sioner. This money was paid in wages, and when it was considered that the bankrupts had employed as many aS 150 men it was nothine extraordinary that such a sum had been drawn. It could not be proved that the money had gone anywhere else. These men were pen .iless now. It had beee alleged by some creditors that the bankrupts had removed a large quantity of goods from the town. As a matter ot fact, he (Mr. Browne) who was then acting on behalf of the trustees, looked into the matter and proof could not be found that one single article had been taken away.We was rather sorry to see the last paragraph which the Official Receiver ended up with. It must be remembered that they were only working men.and that what might appear to be impertinent to the Official Re- ceiver would not be considered impertinent to people in their own station of life. Whilst acting on behalf of the trustees he found daring the latter part of the bank- ruptcy proceedings that the bankrupts gave every B.s9lS- tance they could possibly render.Ueder the circumstances he submitted that as they had been 11 years bankrupts that an order for a small number of years would satisfy the conscience of the Bankruptcy Act—if it had one— and also that of the Official Receiver. His Honour said all the facts which had been stated by Mr. Browne would not alter the course he ought to take in this case. He considered it a bad case. Ignor- ance and want of education was absolutely no excuse whatever. When men chose to embark in business of , this kind they must take care to carry it on on business lines. From 11 at to last, never in any instance that could be shown, had they conducted it in a business-like way. They had never kept any books of account,never ascertained how they stood, and never knew how far they were justified in going on. The conclusions which the Official Receiver had come to were abundently supported by the evidence, and there were no facts before the Court contradicting the facts upon which the Official Ritodver based his re- port. These men embarked in speculation,notbing more nor less. The conclusions which the Official Receiver drew were very serious conclusions, and the trade and business of the country would be thoroughly upset and unsound if men carried on business in the manner which these two men had been guilty of. It was abundantly proved that they continued to trade when they knew they were insolvent. They were really insolvent right at the very beginning because they had no capital to commence with. They had been guilty of misconduct in that respect. From the very first their speculatione were rash and hazardous. They had also given undue prefer- ence to certain creditors in order to stave off proceed- ings and to enable them to get further credit. But that was not the most serious offence. He regretted with Mr. Browne that the Official Receiver bad been obliged to make the report in the concluding para- graph as to the bankrupts treating their position some- what flippantly,and one of the bankrupts being inclined to be impertinent. It was perhaps not surprising to hear that when they knew these men were in such a desperate position as they were. One of the great objects of the Bankruptcy Act was to purge the trades of the country of men who ought not to have occupied positions which they chose to assume. The two men in this case had never shown themselves to be men who ought to have embarked in considerable busi• nose. From first to last their whole trade had been one of speculation, and if they had succeeded they would have come out of it rich men instead of poor men. Eveuts went against them and they entered the Bank- ruptcy Court. He did not think that be oaght to allow them to continue in the trade again. If business were permitted to be carried on in the way these men bad conducted it, the whole commercial business of this country, whether foreign or home trade, would be most seriously shaken and disturbed. He thought he could not do otherwise than refuse this application alto' gether. Mr. Browne : Will you give me leave tO apply
further? His Honour : Ns, I should suggest to your clients to return to the trade which they had previously filled with success.

'rag iticton AND THE HISPANO-AMERICAN WAR. At the Parish Church, on Sunday night, the Rector the Rev. Canon Willis, preaching from the words " A time of war and a time of peace." Ecclesiastes iii. 8, said they were just passing through what should be a semen of peace, but within the last few days they had been aroused to the sound of war. They had been expecting it, but they had been hoping that it might pass away and that wiser counsels might prevail. But war had broken out, and he supposed it was a subject that was in everybody's mind at the present moment. What were the ca ees of this war ? So far as they coold tell, there had been sad mis-governmeat in Cuba daring the past few years, and the result of this mis- government of the island by the Spaniards had been that a feeling of deep sympathy had been excited with regard to these islanders, and a feeling of fierce indignation against their oppressors. This indignation had perhaps not been wisely expressed, and it had brought about retaliation. Demands had been made to the Spaniards which it was difficult for a high-spirited nation to concede. The consequences of war were terrible, and it was an awful thing to rush lightly into war. They had had assurances from both sides that it was with no light heart that either nation took part in the war. The war would result in death and much suffering. It was very easy for the populace to cry war, but what an awful thing for those soldiers and sailors who had to fight the battles ! Some were killed, and many were maimed, and perhaps would have to en- dure life-long suffering. There would also be a perpetual feeling of resentment on the part of the vanquished against their conquerors, and much sorrow would fall on the survivors and friends of the dead and wounded. He could remember what happened after the Crimean war and Indian Mutiny. They could hardly Pass along the street without seeing people in mourning. Hardly a family but lost a relation in these wars. Those who were engaged in commerce with Cuba would suffer pecuniary lose, and there would be general inconveni- ence. There might be, and he hoped there would be, good results front the war. They believed that all things were overruled by providence. This would be the first naval engagement in modern warfare. In the war be- tween Japan and China the Japanese navy Was equipped with modern apeliances, but the Chinese was not. Both ' Spain and America had fine vessels, and a naval engage- ment between them would afford a great deal of infor- mation. Perhaps it wou'd result in nations being more and more averse to war when they saw what terrible consequences occur .1, and it mien?' also be a lesson to other nations that no nation could govern badly with impunity. England most observe strict neutrality and impartiality, and when the time came we might be able to render cline kindly offiles to tooth sides. WYCLIFFE P S.A 80-;IE CY. There was an anCe•ciab'e falling-off in the attendance at the me-ring of this society on Sunday afternoon, die no deuht to several counter-attractions, and to the ex- ceptianally fl le weather. Mr. Francis Brown, of War- rington, was the chairman and addressed him.eit more particulary to the twiny men in the congregation. He spoke on the infiaence of companions upon behaviour, and advised young men to be careful whom they asso- ciated with, He also gave some good advice on how to "get on." Mr. flolyoake, of Manchester, delivered the address, and in an address on " Love "he referred to it as the greatest force in the! world. Mr. Pearce was tne soloist, and gave an effective ren ering of "0 God have mercy." Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ. The service was also taken pelt in by Mr. A. Lang and Mr. Robbins. WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. This annual event took place on Sunday, and though perhaps not so satisfactory from a pecuniary point of view,it passed off successfully. The Rev. H. T.Spencer, M.A., M.Sc., of Wavartree, was the preacher for the oc- cseion,whe it may be stated in passing, was formerly a teacher at the school during hi; residence in Warrington for a number of years. At the morning service the children from the school were accommodated in the galleries,and they sweetly sang a number of hymns and the chant "The strain upraise." The choir gave an effective rendering of the anthem "The Lord is my strength" (H. Sinart). Solos were sung during the ser- vice by Mrs. Gleave,Miss E. Knewles,Miss Booth,Mr. A. Griffiths, and Mr. W. H. Wallington. Toe preacher based his remarks on the text" 0 Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped, add ye year to year ; let the feast; come round." Isaiah 2) chap, let verse (revised version). He explained that Biblical scholars were not agreed as to the exact meaning to be attached to the word And which referred to Jerusalem. He printed out that by some it was ascribed to mean the hearth of God, by others the temple of God, and further by others, the lion of God. The preacher proceeded to apply these several meanings as symbolical of the Sunday school, and in doing so briefly referred to his connection with Wycliffe Sunday School, In the after- noon commencing at 2.30, a scholar's service was con- ducted in Wycliffe Flail. by the Superintendent, Mr. George Wallington. Special hymns were sung by the scholars, and Mrs. A. Booth sang a solo entitled" The Children's Home." I most interesting address on " Sincerity " was delivered by Mr. Spencer. At the evening service there was a large congregation. The service commenced with the singing of the anthem" 0 Gladsome Light "(Sullivan) by the choir, and later in the evening they also rendered "There is a Green Hill," (Gounod). In the latter Mr. R. H. Pearson very effi- ciently sang the solo. Mr. George Wallington conducted the singing, and Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ with his accustomed ability. The preacher took as his text " Neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the Lord my God of that which doth cost me nothing." (II Samuel 24 chap, 24- verse). Be printed out that one reason why their offerings to God should cost them something was because of the great coat God did evrrything for their benefit. He enumerated various wave in which they could give to God that which cost them something as by r.,,ifrs of money, by worship, by testimony, and by service. Collections were taken at each service on be- i half of the Sunday school funds, the total amount col- lected being £39.

ANOTHER NEGLECTED HOME AT WARRINGTON:,

On Friday Damming at the Warrington Police Court before the Mayor and other magistrates, John O'Niel' and Mary O'Neil. 5, Appleton-street, were charged , with haying on the 14th April neglected their children, Frank, Charlotte, Annie, James Henry. , and Sarah Jane. Inspector McAteer, N.S.P.C.C., prosecuted and said that the defendants were the arents of five children, and were charged with neg- lectig all of them. In consequence of a report he re- ceivpd he visited the defendants house on Thursday in nomopany with P.C. Chrirnes and found James Henry &ado Sarah Jane, two of the children in the house. He examined them and found them insufficiently clothed and very duty. The howe was poorly furnished. In the front bedroom, occupied by the defendants and the twe youngest children, they found a rickety bedstead covered with a mattress and tick. The only bed covering was a couple of old worn garments The floor looked as if It had never been either washed or brushed ; and the house smelt offeneively. The hack bedroom, which was occupied by the other three children, contained a smedl bed made up of a quantity of straw, and no bed-clothes whatever, it was very filthy. The female defendant told bins that drink was the cause of the con- dition of the hew. On the 16th witness called again and found the male defendant asleep by the fire and half drunk. Ile woman had a black eye. All she had done was to partly sweep the front roorn.—P.C. Chrimes corroborated the statement of the Inspector.— O'Niel said be worked at Bewsey Forge and could onli earn ss. a day. Be had been without work many weeks since Christmas.—The ma.istrates adjourned the case for a month in order to give the defendants a chance of improving the condition of the children and home. BICYCLE RIDINO IN BRIDGE-STREET.—EXTELkONDINIAY SPICED.

Samuel Tilling, a young man living at 14, Napier-et., was charged at the Warrioeton Borough Police Court on Wm.:ay, with havidg on the 1.13rh April furiously ridden a biceee in Bridge-street to the danger of passengers.— P.C. Beeped&le proved the case. He said he was stand- ing at Bridge-foot at a quarter to eight in the evening when the defendant passed him on his bicycle, and went up Bridereestreet at the rate of from 12 to 14 miles an hour. The defendant rang no bell.—The Chief Con- stable: Thi, is lee of the most dangerous parts of the town, and Bridge-street is one of the streets with regard to which the Town Clerk some time ago posted notices to the effect that bicyclists were not to go more than six miles an hour over it.—The Mayor: That is so. —lnspector Greatrex corroborated the evidence of the police officer, and estimated the speed at which the defendant was travelling at from 18 to IE3 miles an hour. one of the wheels of the machine touched witness's clothes. The defendant " had no whistle" no lamp, no anything, and went past him like a flash of lightning."—Defendant said he had been to Delatnere Forest, and as he could net get up Mersey-street, as it was PO crowded, he went up Bridge-street. A horse and cart were following him, and he was obliged to get out I of the way, but he was not going fast, although it might appear to the officer to the contrary.—The Mayor: But you have said nothing to justify you in going at such a furious pace. I have not a word to say against cyclists, and I like to see them enjoy themselves, but I I have had many narrow escapes myself, and it is exceed- iugly dangerous to travel through the streets of War- rington at more than six or seven miles an hour. Rapid riding will have tube put down, and I for one am strongly opposed to it. We could fine you 40s , hut ou this occasion we have decided to fine you only Si. in- cluding costs. DESERTION BY A FATHER. At the Borough Felice Court on Mondar, before the Mayor, and other magistrates, Edward Sauce, an old offender, was charged with rinsing away from War- rington leaving his child chargeable to the common fuod of the Warrington Union.—Mr. Basil Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians, and said the prisoner's child was four years of age, and had been deserted by its father. A warrant was taken out for prisoner's appre- hension on Fehruary 17th, and it hal been in the hands Of the police since. Be was apprehended on Friday or Saturday at Leigh with coniderable difficulty. Oa the, 28th October last year the prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour for a similar offence in refer- ence to the same child. It had then been in the work- : house several months. The prisoner bad evidently made up his mind not to keep his child. He was a widowev.— The Chief Constable said the police had experienced the utmost difficulty in apprehending Sauce. He had eluded them by every possible device in his power, and when he was apprehended at Leigh he stuck out that his name was O'Brien,and threatened all sorts of pains and penal- ties for false arrest. This was his 34th appearance.—ln answer to Aldermar, blackhurst. Mr. Shearer said the Cost to the union in the present case was about 50s.— The Chief Constable added that the prisoner bad been charged with assaulting his wife and the police. He had been imprisoned several times. Ho had had six month, for an aggravated aesaiilt.—Prisone r : lam willing to pay the money.—The Clerk : It is net now a question of inoney.—Mr. Shearer : I could no': compromise the matter now if the prisoner consented to pay the amount down.—Sauce was seat to prison for two months with hard labour.

THEFT FROM A FELLOW LODGER. On Monday at the Warrington Borough eolice Court, before the Mayor and othor magistrates, John Hall, hawker, last of Wigan, and William Maybe'', hawker, Southport, were charged, the first with stealing and the second with receiving the sum of 103. from John Flem- ing at Plinston's lodging house.—Flemingr, who resided at Plinston's lodging house, said the mooey was paid to him as his wages. Ile could identify the money as one of the half crowns was marked with a spot of blood. He noticed it as he put it into his pocket on Saturday night. One of the prisoners slrpt in the next bed to , him, Witness placed the trousers under his pillow. In the morning be found the trousers on the side of his bed and the money gone. The same side on which Hall's bed wag- Be informed the Isndlord.—Sergeant Taylor said be received tho report of the theft from the witness Fleming. He took the two men into custody in conse- quence information received.—The Chief Con- staevidence. The pr were committed bte also o f the g gave ve prisoners w to pr onth wirb hard labour. WARRING TON BOROUGH POLICE_ COURT:

- --- FRIDA.y.-Before the Mayor (Alderman John Edward Wright). in the chair, Councillor EL Roberts, Councillor James Smethurst. and Dr. Gornall. A. DEF ki7LTING APPRENTICE -14liza Garrett 24. Dale- street, was summoned by Messrs. Platt Wilkinson and Co., with neglecting to work according to her indentures -Mr. Brown who appeared on behelf of the complainants, said although the claim 1,218 only for 2s it involved a point which was of great moment. The defendant Eliza Garrett. had with others bBO enticed away from their work. The reason put ferward was that she wss not 14 years of age until July of the year she was bound, and her indentures d tted from May. The magistr ttes ;create tan order for the defendant to return to her work, and if her mather dispute 1 the terms of the indentures, she was to bring the ease up again. MONDAY.- Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderm Harri- son. Franc(mb and Blackhurct ; Councillors Smethurst and Shaw Green, and Messrs. Birchen and Wright. DtFrunsaacs: BY A SOLDIEI.—John William Travis, a Private of the South Lancashire Regiment stational at Orford Barracks. was charged with having been drunk end silsor- derly in Winwick-road on Saturday night.-He pleaded guilty.-P.C. Dawson proved the ease. ore said he wee on duty on the night in question when he received intimation that a disturbance was going on in Winwick-road. He pro- ceeded there and found the prisoner on the ground. He was not only drunk, bat was making use of very bad language. He advised him to return to the Barracks, but as he refused he was obliged to take him into custody. He was very rough. -The prisoner said he was given no chance to go borne-Tile Chef Constable I thought we had finished with 'Travis when he joined the Army, but apparently we have not done so. He had been in the army before, but was evidently discharged with ignomony. However, Irs contrived to enter the army again on some pretext or another. He was a bic nuisance whilst he was a civihan.-Councillor Shaw Green t I thought the army authorities would not receive inch a man.-Mr. Talbot They would not if they had known his character. He is liable to be prosecuted for mak- ing a fain, attestation.-A fine of 10s. was inflicted. DRUNK AWE DISORDERLY. -George Ward, a carter. was I charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night the 16th April, in Hylands-street.-Fined 105. and costs, - Elizabeth Dutton. for the same offence on the 18th April In Parker-street, was fined ss. and costs, er in default 14 days' hard labour. _ .

A Row IN MERSEY- P. W. Humphreys was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and William Brain- hall with making use of obscene language. The two were fighting In Mersev-street after a dil;iute about football. Bramhall was fined ss. and costs, and Humphreys 2s. 6d. and costs. _ . _

A NEGLECTFUL FATHER SENT TO GAIL —Thomas eloynes, last of Angel-street, fanchester, was charged with running a'svay from the borough, leaving his wife isnot two children. Mr. Shearer.who prosecuted on behalf of the Union. said the prisoner's wife was maintaining herself in Frodsham.—The Chief Constable said the man was apprehended in Man- chester. This was his 10th appearance for different charges. Cloynes was comtnited for three months' hard labour. DRUNK AND DIBORDERLY.—JuIia Ann Shields was charged with is, ing drunk and disorderly on Tuesday night.—P.C. Crimes proved the case. This was her 42nd appearance. She was sentenced to one months' hard labo ir, TROUBLE FOR A. ANOTHER LAD 70It THE " CLIO."— Richard McCue, brick- layer, 172 Longford-at., was summoned for the non-atten- dance of his son at school.—McCue explained he was the stepfather of the lad aud al-o of three other children. He had done all he possibly could for him. The lad would sleep out at night, and he had no control over him. He was the oldest of his step-children and eleven years of age. He was afraid the lad would spoil the others.—The Chief Constable said the lad was incorrigable, and exercised a contaminating Influence over others. McCue was not to blame for the lad —The magistrates explained that although they did not think he was responsible for the lad's behaviour, they wowd not sead any more of his children to the " Clio." The semi-final between these teain,. was played off on Monday evening, in splendid weather, before about 3,000 spectators. Neither team had any advantage in regard to wind. as there was none to speak of. Cros- field's kicked offi, and a very faet game commenced. Rylands' had a younger brother of Smack Bate as one of their backs. Cresfielde forwards appeared stronger and faster than the Iran- workers, though Rylands' seemed to have the advantarte in the backs. The soap men probably through their better forwards, did most of the pressing. After fifteen minutes play, Rylands began to show up better. The backs followed up well, and an almost cer- tain try was missed by the ball skidding away from the men. The advantage was of very short duration, for she soapworkers again began to shine, giving the wire men plenty to do to keep them from scoring. Some smart play by Crosfield's forwards eaded in a try being secured by Dunbobin,the effort to convert being a failure. This was still the score when half-time shortly afterwards came. When play was resumed a closely conteted struggle began. The wire workers shewed a bit of good play, the hacks following up splendidly, though nothing resulted after some desperate play before the goal posts. Crosfield's did the pressing, after this, the ironworker, play being to keep them from scoring. The consistent play of the soapworkers had its reward in a neat place goal by Harris. This evidently roused the wire workers For they began to show play which would have affected the result, materially, earlier on in the game. r arising splendidly the forwards teak the ball up the field in a manner not to be denied, the backs mean- while following up finely. The resulc was a try being secured by Newton for the wire-men. But three minutes play was now left and the game was concluded without any further score. div.head: SHIP CANAL
div.p: SHIP CANAL
RAILWAY COMPETITION. REDUCTION OF RAILWAY RATES.

The Pall Mall Gazette says :-111 the railway com- panies which carry merchandise between the Metropolis and Cottonopolis have just issued to their customers, the manufacturers and merchants at both ends, a cir- cular announcing that the curiae° ou cotton and linen fabrics packed in bales, cases, trustie, and packs te and from the two cities will be reduced from 40s. to 30s. ptir ton from May 2nd to December 31st of the current year. It is added that the recluetien in question is an " experimental " one,tand some traders think that if by the present reduction of 25 per cent, the railway com- paniee could starve off the steamship companies which have, since the opening of the Ship Canal in January, 1894, conveyed goods direct from Manchester to London, then the railways would put up the rate to the old level —certainly a high one, against which the horns trade houses in particular, as well as the Far Eastern shippers, have pretested for years. However, the steamship csnmanies have been carrying the merchandise named at 225. 6d. per ton, iucluding collection and delivery, which is generally considered to be a fair rate, and allowing little margin for reduction to meet this tardy move on the part of the railway companies. The latter may possibly divert some of the more urgent traffic from the sea route at the comparatively small difference which now exists between the two, hut traders whn have been regularly receiving the benefit of the appreci- able saving on the carriage by sea as compared with rail , since the opening of the Ship Canal will, doubtless stick to th., water carriage, even with no reduction on the 225. (11, rate, in the case of goods which are not required to he moved quickly. Ship Canal supporters will net, however, view this development with any particular delight.

TRAP ACCIDENT —On Monday evening an accident occurred on the railway bridge near the station to Mr. Thomas rtirchall, Church-street, Warrington. Mr. Bir- chall was rrturning to Warrington with a horse and cart when an express train passed and caused the animal tc bolt. The driver endeavoured to bring the animal to a standstill but in doing so the reins brokettte result being that Mr. liirchall wag thrown to the ground receiving injuries to ale chest and leg. Efe afterwards Continued his journey to Warrington where his injuries were at. tended to by Dr. McCarthy. ACCIDENT AT CHRIST CHURCH.—OR Sunder evening a young lady from Warrington, who was attending service at Christ Church felt unwell and attempted to leave the church. Upon arriving near the direr however, she fainted and fell, her head coming in contact with the latch of the door, which caused a nasty gash on the left temple. Members of the congregation rendered assist- ance and removed the lady to the heuse of Mr. Henry Antrobus,sextcn. A cab was afterwards sent for and the injured person conveyed to her home in town. The in- cident naturally caused some excitement in the church.

RUNCORN V. WIDNES. Runcorn visited Widnes on Saturday, and had a friendly game with the footballers of that town. Net much interest was taken in the event and there was only a poor attendance. The ground was hard and in bed cendition. Farmer started for Runcorn. Peacock re- turred, Butterworth replying to touch at half way. From the touch kick Jolley stemmed a rush by the he roe forward,. Some good p-eeeing between Faulkner and Butterwertla was not productive, the result ot some vieoroue play by the home forwards and Houghtoa. in attempting to get away was stormed by AePeY• rbe exchanges continued to be fought in the Run- corn half, Houehton making a in irk, and Wilkin- son cleverly got to the centre. Jolley marking from Nevitt's return, and smart passing by this visitors gained them considerable ground, Peaceck kicking to ball way. When close in Faulkner and Walker made an attempt to pierce their way through. Alford was the stumbling block, and play reverted to the Runeorn half, Offside saw the visitors penalised, but Houghton ran grandly along the touch. The Widnes, eight made a united rush to the line, the ball going into touch clogs in, Wilkineon stopped Grace, who was again going ‘vell and Rispau taking the ball shoe at goal without effeotine any damage, the oval going dead. Alferd tried hie luck with a drop without success, and Aspry made a mark frnn which Realms nearly kicked a goal. Grace was afterwards conspicuous, and Houetiton was tackled by Handley. Houghton kicked at goal from a free kick, but the ball did not rise. &slop was applauded for , tricky play. Final result :—Widaes, 2 points, Runcorn, nil. svARRINGToN AV. It proved to be of a rather one-tided character,the home team win- ning by 34 points to nil. Scott was in grand form for the home team, and scored ne fewer than tour tries. Birkenhead put the ball in motion, and some nice open play was witnessed during the first ten mieutes, War- rington if anything having slightly the best of the open- ing stages. The recipents of the prizes responded in suitable terms A resume of the season was given by Mr. Etetwood, who stated, that though this was the club's first aeabon,they had been surprisingly successful and could hold their own against any team of novice& brought against them. One of their members,T.Devlin.- had gained the distinction of carrying away the splendid gold medal for first man home against three other clubs, in an invitation at Ashton-in-Makerfield. This was his first season at the sport, and he would doubtless be heard of in future. As regarded the future,he said their prospects were of the brightest, a good secretary and treasurer, a good committee, and better still, the sub- stantial balance in hand of nearly Le. (Applause.) Votes of thanks were passed to the chairman for his services, and to Mr. Llewellyn for his attentiveness to their comfort during the season. Mr. H. Jones officiated at the iianoforte. The officials for the next season are : secretary,J.A. Watsoti; treasurer,J.G. Basketter;captain. G. Eastwood; vice-captain, John Potts.

div.head: CAUSES AND CRISES.
div.p: CAUSES AND CRISES.

" Lay hands suddenly on no man," says St. Paul in his charge to Timothy." A wise and an excellent piece of advice. In all the important affairs of life it is well to make haste slowly. The mysterious power which we• call Nature marks her large management of things by gentleness, firmness, and deliberation. No power or• "pull" on earth can make the suit rise nne second ahead of his time or hasten the end of an ephemera whose 4 career covers but an hour or two at the longest. To be sure men perish suddenly by accident, but, properly un- derstoodosever by disease. Even those attacks which are swiftly fatal—such as of ipoplexy or heart failure— are always a long time in preparation. A volcanic erup- tion may become overwhelmingly violent in a few days,. but the mountain has been perhaps a hundred years getting ready for such a tremendous demonstration. So, I say again, it is with these aboorissnl po- tencies which we group together under the general term disease. No one falls suddenly from bier health into a state of chronic pain and suffering. There is a sort of instinct in these wonderful bodies of ours' which leads them to see and resist the oncoming of any Illness. And if we were sufficiently observant and intel- ligent to note the early signs of this antagonism, and to, help the unthinking system to make its prelim:tinesl fight, we should never have those dreadful experiecoell which make the history of the race one of distress sad woe. Our lives would be longer and happier and !Fe- -1 should pus away at last as the orb of day does, fading gradually into a night cool and clear, and studded with the eternal stars. A lady, whose name will appear pre- sently, tells a tale which illustrates this point. Let cro ,read It and try to deduce some practical wisdom from the facts it sets forth.

, "In the spring al 1832," she says, "I felt done up and Ilpod for nothing. Without knowing how I came eo, was tired and languid. Tho least exercise or exertion I was too much for me. I had a bad taste in the mouth.. my appetite was poor, and after eating the simplest food I felt an awful burning pain in the stomach,and I had & load on the chest as if it were an actual weight. "I was P.onstaßtly belching up a sour fluid, and tbe wind would rise into ay throat forming what seemed like a ball, until I was nearly choked. Something ap- peared to be eating my stomach away. Then a severe pain settled in my left side, and my heart beat in that the noise of it was loud as the ticking of a clock. My breathing was hard and difficult, and I could walk only a few yards without stopping to rest.

"At night I got no proper sleep, for I was never easy unless propped up with pillowe—almast sitting up in bed. My breathing at length got so bad that I bad a bed made up in the sitting-room, where there was a fire, and for seven years I slept downstairs.

"For months togsther I was unable to leave my bed. I was much troubled with cold hands and feat ; and sometimes cold, clammy sweats broke out all over me and I shivered until the bed shook beneath me. " As time went on I became se low, weak and nervon that I could scarcely move about ; and if anyone walked' across the floor the shaking upset me. I was particu- larly alarmed at the constant burning pain in my stomach, for my mother died of cancer. and I feared was going the same way. With 'varying experience I continued in this wretched condition over eleven years. My sufferings were more than tongue can tell. During this long and gloomy time I had one doctor after an-- other, but never obtained more than temporary ease. One doctor said I had too much blood on the stomach, and others said different things. Since then I have- hen free from pain and able to do my housework with ease. It has made rue a new wr)tn so. You have my consent to publish my letter, and I will answer inquiries.
