div.head: MARRIAGE OF MISS IS &BEL REYNOLDS.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MISS IS &BEL REYNOLDS.
FASHIONABLE FUNCTION AT DA YEN HAM.

The picturesque little village of Davenham wore its gayest aspect on Wednesday last week, when the marriage of representatives of two well-known Cheshire families was solemnised, in the presence of an aristocratic assembly and a crowd of villagers at the Parish Church. The contracting parties wine Mr. Frederick William Toler, son of Mr. John Toler, of Salterstord Hall, Holmes Chapel, and Miss Isabel Reynolds, fifth daughter of the late Captain Rey nolds and Mrs. Reynolds, of Raddon Court, Latch ford, near Warrington, and Whatcroft Hall, near Davenham. The Reynolds family have resided at Whatcroft for two years, having removed thither from Raddon Court, and they are now held in as high esteem in their rural home as they have been for years in the towu of Warrington. This being the case it was not surprising that on every hand there should be evidence that an unusual amount of inter- est was manifested in the event,and that all joined in hearty good wishes to the bride and bridegroom The decorations, testifying as they invariably do on such occasions to the goodwill of the inhabitants, were on an exten.ive and artistic scale. Commence- ing with the hall itself, the front was gay with many coloured flags,which floated from every point of vantage. Spanning the entrance to the lawn was a beautiful triple arch of evergreens,spangled with yellow,red, and other flowers, fringed with flowers and festoons,and surmounted with four flags. This was the work of Mr. Byron, the head gardener, and his assistants, Messrs. Alcock, Bond and Shaw. At intervals along the drive, small flags dotted the green sward. Just over the canal bridge, Mr. John Stubbs (Manor Farm), and Mr. Thomas Shaw (Brook House Farm) bad erected a very nice arch, bearing on the scrolls "May this union be one of love," and f' God bless the Bridegroom,' , The supports were entwined with gorse, while at the cp was arranged a cluster ot figs with a fancy paper crown in the centre. Coming to the top of Shipbrook Hill, Mr. James Parry and his daughters, assisted by t, e workmen, had erected a very nice arch, bearing on the scrolls adorned with heather, gorse, and a few bunches of laurels. On the had side were the words "Health, wealth, and happiness,"and on the ethers " Daly your days be long and happy." Surmounting the whole was a Scotch fir bush, gaily dressed with flowers of different shades. There was also a pretty side arch, and streamers were secured along both sides. "God Bless the Union," and "None but the brave deserve the fair," were the appropriate words set forth on a very neatly constructed arch a little further down the lane. This was the work of Mr. Ambrose }leashed: The supports were covered with gorse, and the trellis-work in the centre was em- bellished with evergreens and rosettes. A crown of fancy paper overtopped the whole. Opposite the church gates Mr. Edward France-Hayhurst bad caused to be erected an elaborate double trellis-work arch, the scroll piece of which took the form of the crest of the Reynolds family —a fox and gate. Evergreens, gorse, flowers, etc., prettily bedecked the erection. The entrance to the churchyard was bright with parti-coloured .fl while the Royal standard floated from the church tower, and in the school and at other places in the village,bunting, etc., was displayed.

div.head: AT TEE CHIMCH.
div.p: AT TEE CHIMCH.

Two o'clock was the hour fixed for the ceremony, and long before the earliest guests began to arrive the approaches to the church were thronged with eager spectators. It was in every respect a brilliant function, and the dresses worn by the eutsts were lovely produc- tions. Mrs. Reynolds (the bride's mother) was dressed in a black and white striped silk, her bouquet being of white rases and lilies. Mrs. Snowdon was gowned in heliotrope canvas, over silk foundation ; and Miss Reynolds looked well in lawn canvas, trimmed with ter- quoise blue and steel ornaments, her dainty leghorn bat being trimmed with sense roses and velvet. Mrs. France Hayhurst (Bostock Hall) was attired in a striped dress of Paris blue and black, with collar of royal blue velvet, edged with fur, and front of embroidered silk, and with toque to match. Mrs. Wyatt had a pretty dress of Parma blue, with hat trimmed with tulle and flowers to match ; and Mrs. Inman wore a grey costume trimmed with silver braid. Mrs. Browne wore a dainty ' blue, trimmed with cream guipure lace, and a plumed toque. A lovely dre's of silk muslin delaine, with plain green silk belt, was worn by Miss Verdict Cooke. Miss Verdin (the Brockhurst) was dressed in figured black silk, and Miss Turner (Over Hall) wore Parma violet blue, trimmed with cream. The period of waiting was spent by the lady members of the throng in admiring the dresses and in listening to ' the sweet strains of music rendered on the organ by Mr. T J. Candlin. The arrival of the bridal party caused a 'd. %ter of excitement amongst the congregation, and as " e strains of" Lohengrin's ' bridal music pealed from be organ, the brideJeaning on her brother's arm,passed down the aisle and took up ber position at the altar steps. ffier dress was of dainty ivory duchesse satin, trimmed with rare old Limerick lace, with Watteau train. She wore her mother's veil, which was of net, handsomely embroidered, and her ornaments included a diamond crescent, the gift of the bridegroom. In her hand was a magnificent shower banquet of lilies of the valley, camellia, and other white blooms. Her attend- ant bridesmaids were the Misses Sylvia, Joan' and Dorothy Reynolds, her sisters, and Mies A. M. C. Toler, sister of the bridegroom. They were attired in pretty dresses of Brussels net, over rose-pink silk under-skirts. Their hats were of bronze straw, trimmed with pink roses, and each wore a gold safety-pin brooch, with diamond initials, and carried bouquets of pink roses and mignonette, the gifts of the bridegroom. The Rev. H. G. Barnacle vicar of Holmes Chapel, solemnized the nuptials, and was assisted by the Rev. T. W. H. France- Hayhurst, rector of Davenham. The service was fully choral. The surpliced choir sang the hymns, " The King of Love," and "The voice that breathed o'er Eden," and chanted the proper psalm. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. Sylvanus Reynolds, and the duties of the best man were discharged by Mr. C.M. Sing.

AT WOATCIIOFT HALL. Mendelssehn's " Wedding March" was played as the happy couple left the. church, the bells in the steeple clanging forth their peal. Showers of rice and confetti greeted the couple,and they drove to Whatcroft Hall, where a reception was held. The following is a list of the invited guests,some of whom were unable to be present :—Mr and Mrs A'oxander, Mr W G Armits- stead,ldr and Mrs Armitstead, Miss Aldersey, Mr and Mrs H Armitstead, Mr and Mrs Alfred Ashton, De and Mrs Ii T Browne, Mr W D Bullock, Mr and Mrs Border. The bride's travelling dress was of Paris blue canvas, trimmed with white (Cliff on, with blue straw hat, trimmed with chiffon and lace, and white plumes to match.

PANIC IN PARR HALL.—FALSE ALARM OF FIRE. A panic took place on 6unday evening at Farr Hall, where Dr. Vint and his Globe choir were giv- ing a sacred concert. A solo was being sung and for the purpose of illustrating the same on the screen, the lights were turned low. The time was about 20 minutes past nine, and there would be 1 1,200 people present. A young woman in the gal- lery was seized with a fit, and during the excite- ment which followed, some one foolishly called out " Fire I Fire I" The reason of this exclamation is not known, as there was not the slightest cause for alarm. The result, however, NVErS, that the majority of the audience at once rose and vacated their seats end there was a rush for the street. Some one called for the lights to be turned up, but this was not done at once. Some 300 people gained the Street. Dr. Vint who showed great presence of mind told the audience that there was not the slightest need for alarm, and asked them to resume their seats, which they had when the lights were tarried up. Those who had got into the street returned to the hall, and the performance was proceeded with. We understand one man was injured slightly by another, in his rush to pass him on his way to the door

div.head: letters to tne Otttor.
div.p: letters to tne Otttor.
ALDERMAN SUTTON AND CDITNCILLOR H.
ROB ERTe.

Sir,—Althlugh my friend has done his utmost to make ths preseut controversy appear; to your readers as a mere personal quarrel, I respectfully decline to be a party to such a proceeding, or to let the main irsue be lost sight of through the introduction of irrelevant matter. My charge against Mr. Sutton, in brief, is that he has, while holding a seat in the Council as a repre- sentative of the ratepayers, acted in direct opposition to their interests by appearing as a professional witness in the present arbitration case. In his previous letter Mr. Sutton says that he has so acted because he desired to defend the interests of a person whom he (Mr. Sutton) believed was being unfairly and unjustly treated by the Corporation. My suggrstion is that Mr. Sutton has allowed his private and personal interests as a profcs- sional man to override his better sense of his public duties. I also ventured to assert that the proper rule of conduct to observe by anyone finding himself ia such a position as Mr. Suttaa has been placed would be either to give up his public duties er to decline the business which would render his unbiassed salon as a represeotative of the ratepayers impossible. Further I have never said that Mr. Sutton has acted " in what he has done, but what I have said I stand by, viz., that be has acted with grave impro- priety and that he is strongly condemned by the public opinion of the town. The Dunfermline nails fully bears out my contention. The eminent lawyer (Mr. Thomas Shaw, Q.C.) whose advice was sought upon a case pre- cisely similar to our own, while admitting that iu strict law professional men, although members of a Corpora- tion, may recover fees when engaged on behalf of claimants against the Town Council,goes on to say that "serious questions of propriety may manifestly arise in a situation such as that described, but these are for private consideration or for the verdict of public *pinion." Finally my friend says "Mr. Roberts calls upon me to resign my position as an alderman to make room for himeolf." This is really too funny,and reminds me of a story! once read of s parson who told a " coloured member of his con- gregation that he bad been called to another (and better) sphere of labour. Until I am able to " call " Mr. Sutton ill an equally acceptable manner I fear I may Call till I am black in the face, but it will be in vain. Your readers have now got all the facts before them. I My only object is to help to maintain as far as in me I lies the honour and integrity of the public life of my I native town. In this spirit I have acted throughout the present Controversy, and lam well content to leave the matter now to the intelligent judgment of my fellow townsmen.—Yours, &c., H. ROBERTS.

div.head: INTERESTING CEREXIONY AT FRIA.RS'-
div.p: INTERESTING CEREXIONY AT FRIA.RS'-
GREEN.

On Saturday evening a very interesting ceremony took place at Friars -green catapel, Warrington, when Mr. William Brimelow, J.P. of Bolton, and formerly of War- rington, who was accompanied by his wife, unveiled a tablet recording the names of those who have been asso- elated with the church as teachers of the gospel since its establishment, one hundred years ago. The tablet is of beautiful marble, and bears the following inscription : " This tablet records the names of departed brethern who have rendered faithful service to this church, as preachers of the gospel, from the year 1797 :—Richard Harrison. Richard Mills, Peter Reid, Saul Rigby,William McGuinness, Joseph Stout, George Brimelow, John By- rom, Peter Phillips, Joseph Massey, Saul &liner, John Meredith, John McDowell, Joseph Shaw, John Wright, John Roberts, James Gandy,John Green, Edward Twiss, William Farness, James Brimelow."

The proceedings were commenced with tea in the schoolroom, after which the friends assembled in the chapel, where a meeting was held under the presidency of Mr Thomas Barton. After devotional exercime,and brief explanation from the Chairman, Mr. Brimelow,was called upon, and unveiled the tablet amid applause. Re warmly commended the action of the friends of the Church in erecting that tablet. Records of early Inde- pendent Methodist worthies were all too few ; data of their labours and sacrifices were now difficult to obtain; and they were doine well in making a permanent me- morial of the men who founded that church. Inciden- tally, the speaker mentioned that from two of the founders Isaac Mee, whose name appeared on the Trust Deed in 1802, and Richard Mills, one of the preachers— bia wife descended ; whilst as to himself his grandfather was amongst those who withdrew from the Wesleyan Society in 179'7, and the name of his great uncle, George Brimelew, was on the tablet. The speaker proceeded for upwards of an hour, dwelling upon early incidents, characteristic,, and surroundings of the men, whose names were inscribed on the memorial. Referring to the name of Peter Phillips, and associating therewith his 'wife, Hannah, a high tribute was paid to their heroism • and devotion in 1832, when the cholera raged in War- rington, and again in 1847, when the town was smitten by a dreadful fever. Their labours among the poor on these occasions evoked the gratitude of hundreds to whom they ministered for body and soul. Touching upon another prominent name, the Speaker mentioned that Mr. James Gandy's grandfather hospitably enter- tained John Wesley, who preached from his doorstep to .croirds in the market-place. As with the founders so their descendants remained Methodists in doctrine and services: the points on which they differed were as to free service in the ministry and the management of their own affairs as churches. Orieinally they were called ,Quaker Methodists, but since 1810 they had been styled Independent Methodists. In concluding M. Brimelow em3ed the Church to regard the tablet as an impressive 4511 to greater f hfulness, so that they might emulate the heroes whose names were inscribed upon it and hand down to oth,^r7 church heritage of which they were trustees and gear...lan a' 5 not only unimpaired but im- •Proved. Mr. William Hudson followed, cemmenting mon the characteristics and labours of some of the Preachers he had known, mentioning prominently the name of Mr. James Brimelow, father of the preceding tin.Peaker.—Mr. James Evans proposed, and Mr. James --thaseconded, a vote of thank; to the speakers, which wee auopted with acclamation, and the Doxology brought these interesting proceedings to a termination

div.head: WARRINGTON v, BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v, BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS.

The return friendly match between the above clubs was played at Birkenhead on Saturday, in the presence of about a thousand spectators. Beautiful football weather prevailed, and the attendance would have been much larger but for the fact that the Birkenhead crowd had an uneasy at spicion that Warringtou had sent only the" A" team, another club having treated them in this unsportsmanlike fashion the previous Saturday. Both sides were fully represented. The ground was very hard owing to the dry weather and proved by no means suitable for a Rugby game. 34r. S. Williams, of Salford, controlled the following players : Birkenhead Wanderers: Caton,full back ; Liver- sage, Watson,Le wis, and Jones,threequarters ; B ayes and Dillon, half backs; Holmes, Ingham, Griffiths Jones, Glover, Finlan, Pilling, and Edmondson, for- wards.

Warrington: Boscow. full back; Moores, Isher- wood, Duckworth, and Wood, threequarters ; J. T. Bate and IL Bate, half backs; Deakin,Taylor,Naylor, Mason, Fairhurst, Morrison, Barratt, and Saunders, forwards.

Warrington had the assistance of a slight breeze at the commencement. and started the game. Moores returned a kick, and in following up collided with an opponent and was winded. Mason left the forward ranks and went wing, for the time being. Tne Wanderers got the ball out and passing to Jones, the latter attempted to get round Mason but was promptly tackled. Mason sprained his ankle in the tackle and had to leave the field permanently, Moores resuming. These misfortunes robbed Warrington of their sting and the Wanderers made things warm for a brief spell. Jones put in a strong dash for the line and would have got through but for Isherwood chucking him in tmoh at the corner. Moores put Warrington on the aggressive with a neat kick,and J. T. Bate getting away the three-quarters had a chance which Isherwood spliled. The same player made amends with a clinking run te the line and passed to Moores who failed to take the ball. Duckworth had an aboortive drop at goal. Bid kicking on the part of the Wanderers lost them a lot of eround,and the two Bates were a continual source of " Smack " dodged clear agaii and threw to Duckworth who centred and Saunders was tackled with the ball on the line. Tricky play by Moores on the touch line,followed by a punt to the goal line al- most led to a score,the oval going dead a little too soon for Warrington. Lewis and Jones tried a combined movement which was checked in decisive fasldon by Banat:. A penalty against Warrington gave the Wan- derers a chance of opening the scoring but Holmes failed to send the ball over. The homesters scrimmaged on the home line and looked like scoring, but " Smack " Bate stole round the pack and punted clear to the centre. A round of passing by the two Bates, Isherwood and Moores, carried play to the opposite end. Bob Bate got away and passed to Moores who found his course blocked and threw back to " Smack," the latter getting within an ace of the line. Warrington's superior back play be- gan to tell its tale, and ere long the ball travelled ra- pidly through the hands of J. T. Bate, R. Bate, Isher- wood and Duckworth to Wood,who scored smartly near the corner. Duckworth failed to land a goal from the awkward place. Isherwood punted over the home line. sad Caton mulling,the kicker seemed to have scored but had crossed the dead ball line when he grounded. Bob Bate threw wide to Woods who had an easy try at his mercy but knocked on. A mull by Lewis gave Moores an opportunity which he accepted and romped in at his own corner,Deakin failing at goal. More fine passing by Warrington menaced the home line,and " Smack" Bate, Wood, and Dakin carried the ball well up field, Deakin being held. The Warrington seven controlled the packs splendidly.and Isherwood gaves Moores an opening just before ths ;nterval, Moores grounding, but just short of the line. Half time &nivel with Warrington leading by ' two tries to nil. A round of exchange kicking opened the second half, and the advantage lay with Warrington, Caton finding touch too frequently. Fairhurst, Morrison, and Wood handled the leather, but the latter could not gather the , ball before being tackled. Bob Bate handed smartly to Duckworth who punted across to Moores, the latter having hard luck in failing to croes the line. A knock. On spoiled Isherwood's chances similarly, and again the two Bates' had the line at their mercy, but the ball was sent a shade forward. The home lot roamed up and managed to force Warrington back. Lewis received from Watson near the line, but knocked forward just as he was thought to be a scorer. Isherwood and Bate responded with a good run, the former badly judging his transfer to Wood. Again did" Smack " run clean through his opponents, only to find himself unsupported when be had made a beautiful opening. Liversage made a grand effort by himself and almost got through, and altogether the homesters looked likely for pulling the game out of the fire. Moons and Isherwood finally rave Birkenhead a try.the latter failing to catch the ball after the former had kicked backwards, and Finial] grounded near the posts. Watson was unsuccessful with his kick at goal. Wood gave Warrington the upper hand by running Caton in touch. Boscow's centre was accurately judged and was as near bringing about the homestors' downfall as pos- sible. Glover was convicted of unnecessary rougianeas in tackling Duckworth, and received his " marching orders." This equalised the two teams, but the wan- derers put the most energy into their play. Watson ran finely until Isherwood stepped in his path and brought him down. Dillon threw away his chance when scrim- maging under the posts by putting the ball in wrongly. ing p on the Warrington line followed, Jones , missing a try through the ball coming forward to him. Warrington's defence was sound to the close, and they ultimately ran Out winnera by 2 triea (6 points) to the Wanderers 1 try (3 points.)

div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, APRIL 29, ItN9B
EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

POLICE CASES. At Newton Town Hail, uu Monday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, John Urat.hs, of W arrington, was charged with begging at Newton on Sunday night, and was sent to gaol for 14 days. Charles Board- man,of Newton was fined 25.61. and costs for being drunk in Newton on Sunday.

- DEATH OF SERGANT BAG. tIAYDOCK. Very general regret was felt at Haydock when the death of Sergeant Bage was reported on Thurs- day morning. He had been ailing for some time, but the fatal termination of his illness was h.ped against. Sergeant Bap was very popular in the district, where he had been stationed for about 10 years, and his death will be keenly felt by au exten- sive circle of friends. ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN. _ .

--•- - - The annual special services in aid of the District Schools were held in the above church on Sunday. There were very fair congregations at morning and evening service, special anthems being sung by the choir. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. W. E. Jobson who preached appropriate and instructive sermons. In the afternoon an organ recital was given by Mr. Henry W.Radford,organist and choir- master, assisted by Mrs. Brown,as vocalist, and the school children. An excellent programme was sub- mitted, and thoroughly enjoyed, the items being— Organ solo, "Angelic Voices ;" vocal solo, " The IChildren's Home," Mrs. Brown; organ solo." Con- certo, No 9." special hymn, "Little eyes, young and bright," infants ; organ solo," March upon a tneme of Handel ;" " Invocation ;" vocal solo, " Dream of Paradise," Mrs. Brown; organ, " Chant of the Nuns" and "March " (Cornelius). The collections through- out the day amounted to _Ell 55.91

- - - - CLARION CYCLE Wis. The members of this club had a most enjoyable run on Saturday to Childwell and Woolton, near Liverpool. The conditions were very favourable although at times the dust consequent upon the dry condition of the roads proved somewhat incon- venient. Dismounting at Chiidwell the members enjoyed a ramble round the old church yard, where some magnificent monuments are to be seen, especially that of Sir A. B. .Walker which is of an imposing description. After a stay of about half an hour, the party took to the saddle again, and in a few minntea alighted at the Coffee House, Hotel, Woolton, where an excellent tea was partaken of. A game at bowls and a walk round the village and an inspection of the mill which was destroyed by fire a few weeks back terminated the visit. The return journey was commenced shortly after seven o'clock, home being reached about 9 o'clock without mishap. PROPERTY SALE AT EARLESTOWN. At the Viaduct Hotel, Earlestown, on Monday evening, Mr. Gabriel Moon, brought under the hammer three lots of cottage property, by instruc- tion of the Executors of the late Mr. James Elli- son. There was a large company of prospective buyers present, but the biddin,.; was anything but spirited. The first lot consisted of two dwelling. houses, Nos. `..:,26 and 228 Earle-exee,t, in the respec- tive occupations of Mr. James Dean and Mr. Joseph Ellison, together with the gardens thereto belonging and with the large greenhouse attached to 228, the gross yearly rents being £2B 12s, With various offers the bidding rose to £44. at which price it was sold to Mr. Joseph Ellison. Lot 2 consisted of four dwelling-houses, Nos. 17, 19, 21, and 23 in Wood Street, Earlestown, in the respective occupa- tions of Mr. John Ball, Richard Holdman and others, the gross yearly rentals being £4l 12s. Lot 3 comprised five 4 welling-houses adjoining lot 2, and Nos. 25, 27. 29, 31 and 33. Wood-street, in the respective occupations of Mr. Rothwell, C. Buckley and others, the gross yearly rentals being .652. Both these lots were put up together, and realised the sum of £723, the purchaser being Mr. Pownall, farmer, Sankey. VOLUNTEER CHURCH PARADE AT NEWTON. On Sunday the " C" troop of Lancashire hussars, and the two local companies of volunteers attended divine service at St. Peter's Church, Newton. The weather was beautifully fine, and as a consequence large crowdsof people gathered from the villages round about Newton. Cyclists were in evidence, and wagonettes conveyed a many people from Got- borne, Ashton &c. The volunteers paraded at their respective headquarters, the G Company of the 6th , V.B.K.L.R. under the command of Colonel Wood the other officers present being Captain and Lieut.' Smith, the F Company of the 2nd S.L.V.B. being under the command of Major Widdows with Cap. tam n Paterson. Headed by the bugle band, they marched up Church-street into High-street, where they formed up to wait the Husflars. The yeomanry assembled in the Stores yard under the command of 11 Lieuts. Street and S. M. dtrauge,the band under the conductorship of bandmaster Batley, playing op- posite Mr. Pardey's residence, 'The Lost Chord." When all were in formation of fours, they marched to the church where service was held, conducted by the Rev. 11. Monk, vicar. The Church was opened for the first time on Sunday after rebuildingl of the nave, and a largo number of people attended the service. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, ARLESTOWN. The annual special services in aid of the above schools were held in the Chapel on Sunday. Good congregations attended the morning and evening services,and appropriate sermons were preached by the Rev. H. J. Taylor of Southport. At the morning service the choir sang the anthem "Show yourself joyful," and in the evening "Great and marvellous." in the afternoon a musical service was given by the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. W. Banton when the following programme was submitted : Duet and chorus "We are marching onward,"Misse. Baxter; solo, "The golden pathway,' Mr. A. Banton solo, "The two cities," Miss Wood ; anthem, "Grea, and Glorious," choir : solo "There's a Friend for little Children," Mr. J. Webster; solo " Beyond Earth and shadowland," Miss Tombs; Hymn "Such a Loving Friend," choir and children;" solo Mr. A. Banton ; solo and chorus "Looking over Jordan's Stream," Miss M. Stronach; bolo,"Song of Ptiradim," Miss Stronacla ; solo "The Children's Angel," Miss Baxter; solo," Remember Thy Creator,' Mr. J. Webster; anthem "Shew me Thy Ways," choir. Mr. , G. Bunting presided at the harmonium. The col- ections during the day amounted to a little over

div.head: -• ST. PETER'S CHURCH, NRWTON.-lIR OPENING.
div.p: -• ST. PETER'S CHURCH, NRWTON.-lIR OPENING.

St. Peter's Church,Newton, which has been closed for there-building of tlie nave, has so far been com- pleted that it has this week been re-opened for ser- vice. For nearly two years the congregation have worshipped in the Town Hall, Newton, and the transference to the church will be a most agreeable change. It will be remembered that after the death of tte late Colonel McCorquodale, the family inti- mated to the Rev. It. Monk, the vicar of St.Petees, that as a memorial of their late father, they would undertake the restoration of the nave at a cost not exceeding .E 6,000 the plans to be submitted to the family for approval. The contract was let to Messrs. Winnard of Wigan, who have pushed forward the I work with despatch, and the building does them every credit. The style ot architecture is somewhat after the fashion of the old building, but the old tower and gallery have been demolished, and the church presents a more modern appearance. The , oak panelling and carved work has been excellently I carried out,and the lighting arrangements will be found, when it becomes neceesary to bring it into use,to be of an efficient description. At one end just over the choir, the stained window, subscribed for by the local troop of Hussars in memory of the late Sergeant Howard has been placed in position. The old pews have been abolished and the seating is now wholly by chairs. The out- side front of the church has been somewhat altered, and with the abolition of the tower the bell is SUS- pended in a kind of alcove surmounting the clock. Special services were held in the church on Sunday, and on Monday evening a sermon was delivered by the Dean of Chester. On Tuesday afternoon the formal re-opening service was conducted by the Lora Bishop of Liverpool, who was accompanied by his chaplain, Canon Penrhyn, Canon Willis (War- rington),Canon H. St. George (Billings), Revs. E. A. , Duty (Wigan), J. W. Willink (St. Helens), A. A. Markham (W'arrington). T. Richarnson, W. A. Jones (Golborne), E. W. W. Kaye (Newchurch), T. R. Matthews, J. Carson ( argra re). J. B. Jelly (Chor- ley), G. F. Clatke (Daresbury), T. Whitley (Acton Bridge, late vicar of Newton), A. G. Child (Liver- pool), A. Monk-Smith, H. Monk, and J. Rowlands. The ordinary evening service was gone through, after which the Bishop preached from Haggai, 2nd eh part of the 9Lia verse, "The glory of this latter house shall be greater than the former saith the Lord of Hosts." A collection was afterwards madel towards the cost of reversing and renovating the organ, and the new clock. On Wednesday evening the sermon was preached by the Dean of Bangor. div.head: NOTES ON G-A.M.ES AND
div.p: NOTES ON G-A.M.ES AND
ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOT'S/Lt.

Saturday's match was another of the friendly descrip- tion, Birkenhead Wandererr being for the second time Warrington's opponents. The venue was the Birken- head grouad, to reach which the players had te travel both overland and under water—a somewhat novel way of approaching a football match. The trip on tile " underground," though BO much of a novelty was by no means appreeiated, and the players were quick to chow satisfaction when they got ancther glimpse of day- light. A feature of the passage, and one that. was really appreciated, is that the stalun from which one rises to a natural level, li,!a within a few yards of the Wan- deem' ground.

I was one of the first to eater the enclosure, and im- mediately was accosted by a friendly Wanderer,' C3mmitteeman with an anxious face. Showing what I took to be a kindly interest in tne Warrington lot he enquired what sort of a team we had brought. This enquiry I responded to with a detailed description of the shining lights which adorn the world of football and are located at Warrington. The eaquirer next said, with an accent of surprise, "You have not brought the "A" team then? Stockport served us that trick last week." Before I had quite got over the query, a Warrington official chipped in, and at great length expounded the virtues, morals, and unbssmircked purity in general oi the Warrington Committee. Mr. Questioner was so far impressed as to take it for granted that all the interna- tionals were on the team, Spectators however failed to show the same confidence in Warrington's moral rectitude, and only strolled in by twos and threes,

The ground was in a condition scarcely fit for football. Either the hest from below or that from above bad baked the turf in a surface nearly as bard, but consider- ably smoother than Warrington macadam. Before the final whittle sounded there wore many bruises duet. the hard turf. For a few minutes misfortunes fell thick on Warrington. Moores had all the wind knocked out of him before the game was five minutes eld,and Mason on taking his place, sprained an ankle and also retired. This brought the winded on,. bsck again, but for the re- mainder of the afternoon Warriugten played only 14 men.

The Wanderers playe,, a lazy game and before the in- terval a try from both Moores and Wood lay to War- rington's credit. In the second portion, spurred on a few sultry remarks from spectators who had disbursed 61. to see football, the homesters showed up better. A try was scored in a rather flaksy way, and Warrington had to put in all they knew to win. Glover, of the hoeriesters, experimented with Duckworth's equilibrium by endeavouring to stand him on his head, a proceeding which the referee rewarded by sending the experimen- talist off. Time arrived with the score unaltered.

A more important engagement was that on Thursday evening when the Ire league match of the season was played at Widnes. The Chemicals have been breathing threats of vengeance on Warrington for weeks, and nine nut of every ten people anticipated a lively slatieg. for Warrington. The boys in primrose and blue had an idea of their own.and that was to retrieve the Christmas Day disaster. What is caore, they did it. Yes! they really defeated Widnes on chemical soil, "a thing which they had never done before "—I was going to eay,but it is not quite correct. However, it was a thing nobody in Widnes looked for and the dearth uf ensiles later in the evening was sufficient to make one think that there was universal mourning in Widnes. A funny thing about the result is that the homesters were just a point behind at the close. Usually they are that mach is front—see sup- ties.The unexpected does happen at times,and that War- rington should prove themselves the better team as they undoubtedly did, was unexpected.

Predictions looked Uki being fulfilled at first. In six minutes Widnes credited themselves with five points,and there was great rejoicing in the camp. Warring- ton merely redoubled their exertions, and it was a bit of a shock to the sensitive VVidaesian when Moores finished a clever movement with an unmistakable try. No goal accrued, and at half time the homesters held a lead of two points, which was little considering that the wind lad assisted them.

On resumption oae was inclined to think that the visitors had a bit up their sleeves,for the bomesters were outmanouvred fore and aft. rhe Rates, and the rest of the bscks were far ahead of the homesters, and eventu- ally put Moores in possession of another excellent try. At this vage the hamsters looked a beaten team and so they wpm In the whole of the second half they only reaebed the Warrington quarter flag mica, and then if their stay there was sweet, it was very short. Scarcely anyone would credit the news whoa it arrived at War- rington, is unexpected was the result.

It is not at all difficult to find a reason for Warring- ton's success and Widnea's failure:The winners were much tbe better team, and the losers showed a staleness and lack of combination which has been rare with them this season. Brennan was really the only player to do himself justice. Fault could not te found with a single man on the Warrington side, but the actual credit of the victory must be given to "Smack "and Bob Bate. They alto. gather overplayed the home halves, and with Nevitt as slew as possible, and Riven not much better, Isherwood and the rest had a goad time also. Moores played a sterling gams, his two tries being only equalled by his grand tackle of Batey in the second half. Bosco w was Hate as ever, and In the for- wards Morrison was a big and shining light. The nattch altogether was a glorious finish to an inglorious season and raises Warrington three places in the league table.

DEATH OF MR. THOMAS CROSFIELD.

The death occurred on Friday, in his seventy- fourth year, of Mr. Thomas Crosfield, of the firm of Twigge and Crostield,rice millers, of Liverpool,at his residence, 46, Bidston-road, Oxton. Mr. Crosfield was one of a Nonconformist and Liberal family w hich,coming originally from Warrington, has dur- ing a century won a foremost place in commercial circles of Liverpool. For many years Mr. Crosfield was associated with various charitable agencies in the Liverpool district. He was chairman of the committee of the Liverpool Hahnemann Hospital, Hope-street. This hospital was built by Mr. Henry Tate,and opened in 1887, but even before that time Mr.Crosfleld was closely identified with the Horiaceo- pathie Dispensary. lie was one of the leading members of the Society of Friends in Liverpool,and was one of the pioneers in the establishment of the Friends Meeting House, Birkenhead. Other organ- sations which won his sympathies were the Pri- soners' Aid Society and the Howard Society. Apart from his zeal in the works of charity, Mr. Crosfield took a foremost part in public matters and social movements. lie was a prominent member of the Liverpool Peace Socicty,was an earnest and fearless advocate of its aims, and it was only some few weeks ago that he presided over the annual meet- ing of the society at Myrtle-street ohapel. Mr Crosield was a warm advocate of women's suffrage, und his connection with the committee of the Liverpool Temperance Union showe4 him to be a most zealous temperance reformer. Always of a " kind and generous hearted disposition,M.r. Crosfield " will be sorely missed, not only by those who were grat6ful for his charity, but by many who enjoyed the pleasure of his friendship. INTERMENT AT FLAYBRICK HILL.

The interment interment took place on Monday afternoon, at Flaybrick Hill Cemetery. The chief mourners were Mr. and Mrs. H. C. Crosfield (eon and daughter in-law), the Misses Crosfield (daughters), Mr. William Crosfield,Mr.C.J.Crosfield, Mr.l2 C Ryiey,Mr. John Satterthwaite, and Mr. William Satterthwaite, Lancaster (cousins), Mr. and Mrs. William Shaw (son-in-law and daughter), Mr. Frank Rawlins (nephew). Mrs. Deakin (niece), Mr. E. Twigge (Messrs. Twigge and Crosfield), the Misses Twigge, and Mr. George Atkin. Several wreaths were re- ceived from relatives,friends, and organizations with ' which deceased had been connected. Tbe coffin which was of polished American walnut, with silver-plated handles, bore no plate, but the simple inscription, "T. C., 1898," was carved on the lid. The service was conducted by the R9V. E .R. Barrett(Nor wood Congregational (Jhurch,Liverpool) and the Rev. Matthew Stanley (Ozton-road Conger- gationsi Church, Birkenhead). Whilst in the ceme- tery chapel the Rev. Mr. Barrett delivered a touch- ing address, in which he said that by the death of Mr. Crosfield Liverpool had lost a worthy and most useful citizen. Mr. Crosfield was closely identified with many varied forms of Christian and philan- thropic work. In early life he was associated with Ithe Socity of Friends. For more than fifty years 'he was a member of the Liverpool Peace Society, land latterly was vice-president. For forty-one years he was a devoted member of what was now the Liverpool Temperance Union, and probably the Oldest Band of Hope worker in the district. Other organizations which had attracted his sympathies were the Prisoners' Aid Society, the Liverpool Hahnemann Hospital, and the homeopathic dis- pensaries of Liverpool. He had been a prominent member and worker of Norwood Congregational Church from 1876 until quite recently.

UNION OF LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE INSTITUTES,

The ordinary meeting of the Council was held in the Memorial Hall, Manchester, on Tuesday, Mr. Alderman .J. R. Heape (Rochdale) presiding. The Examinations Committee reported that 45 813 papers had been requisitioned in connection with the recent examinations, and 34,159 worked, or 74.5 per cent. as compared with 70.6 per cent. in 1897. - - -

P.:4.A. AT THS Y.M.C.A. There was a tull attendance last Sunday in the Lecture Hall of the Y.M.C. A. and a capital P.S.A. meeting was held. Mr. W. ltoberts presided. Mr. Fort rendered two elarionet solos with taste and skill. Mr. vr.Sand ford was the speaker,his subject being "Life's Duties and Purposes." The President, Mr. Barber,of Manchester, and Mr. Reeves also took part in the meeting.

HARCH OPT OF THE VOLUNTEERS. On Saturday( the Ist Volunteer Battalion, of Warrington turned out under command of Colonel Ridgway in drill order. Accompanied by two bands, they marched to a field on Wilderspool Causeway, kindly lent by Messrs Greenall and Co., where some very interesting movements were carried out under the commanding officer. "The attack" was also practised, the whole lasting nearly two hours after which the battalion was marched home. There were present on parade Colonel J.C. Ridgway, seven officers, and about 200 non- commissioned officers and men. EXHIBITION OF AZALEAS AT WALTON LEA. On Bunday and Monday a large number of people took advantage of Mr. Crosfield's generosity (so often extended) in visiting Walton Lea,the greunde of which had been thrown open to the public for exhibitien of the azaleas. The visitors arrived in every variety of vehicle from the town and all parts of the district. The collection of the azaleas in the greenhouse was altogether uaique. The different varieties were most harmoniously blended, and formed a mass of colour which one might call "kaledeoscopic." It was the general opinion of the visitors that they had never seen a better exhibi- tion, The different plants and fruit trees in the hot-houses were in an advanced state, the whole shewing the great care and attention bestowed upon them by the head gardener, Hr. Kipps.

He dealt with some ot the evil social conditioad of oar time and the) message of Spiritualism in reluion to them. Mr. Bewick fol- lowed with clairvoyance. On Monday evening the meeting was held in the Druid's Hall. Mr. E. Marklew gave an addresa on " Facts versus fancies lin relation to Spiritualism." lie followed his ad- dress with a couple of tests in psychometry.

div.head: REV. E. T. REED.
div.p: THE REV. E. T. REED.

The following is an extract trona—the report of the churchwardens of the Emmanuel Church, Ottawa, Canada, Easter, 1898.—" In November last we welcomed to our midst the Rev. E. T. Reed and Mrs Reed of Warrington, England, and we would wish to take the present opportunity to place on record our appreciation of the kind, faithful and earnest manner in which Mr. Reed has fulfilled his pastoral duties, and of his special efforts put forth for the spiritual welfare of those in this commun- ity. We feel sure we are expressing the feelings of this congregation when we say that although the time is quickly approaching when Mr. and Mrs. Reed will be separated from us by the broad Atlan- tic, their memory will ever live with us, and we trust the good work done by them in this city, will under God's blessing bring forth much fruit."— (Signed) W. Schwitzer, C. T. Kirby, wardens.

div.head: NEW CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THE NEW CHAIRMAN.

Mr, A.hton (the clerk) was voted to the chair pro tem. Mr. Woodward moved that Mr. J. Knowles be chair- man of the Council. Notwithstanding the excellent chairman Mr. J. Mclntyre made, he thought it was an office that should be changed periodically. Mr. Wright seconded. Eh said Mr. Knowles had occupied the chair of the Guardians for a long time and it was only right that he should be exhalted. Mr. Baguley supported the motion, not because the late chairman had not filled the post honourably. Admiral Jones Parry said that la a way, he considered the chairmanship of the Board of Guardians a higher position than that of the Rural District Council. Mr. Rovlance seconded the amendment. - . . .
Mr. Mclntyre: I feel there is a desire for • change and I wish my name to be withdrawn. I have no wish on any consideration to divide the Council.
Admiral Parry : I will not withdraw it. Mr. Spruce also supported the amendment. Admiral Parry ultimately withdrew Mr. Mclntyre's name.
Th,! proposition was put to the meeting and carried nanimously. • - - _ .

Mr. linoWles in taking the chair thanked the mem- bers for the honour they had done him that day. Hs really did not feel inclined to accept the position of chairman of the Roan. of Guardians, as he did not think it Agin. He considered that if there was an honour in it it should go around. As far as being a 1 magistrate he hoped that Mr. Mclntyre would still con- tinue to act as a Justin •of the Peace. He therefore proposed that they petition the proper authorities to have Mr. Mclntyre made a permanent magistrate. Be honed that they would get on with their work very smoothly.
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN.
Mr. Pickering 1;r—o-r poa— and Admiral Jones Parry seconded, that Mr. S. Woodward be vice-chairman. This was agreed to and carried.

NEW _CANAL BRIDGE AT WESTON POINT.

With regard to the bridges crossing the canal at Wes- ton Point, Mr. F. Wiswall, engineer to the Ship Canal Company (Bridgewater undertaking), wrote stating that the company bad decided to reconstruct both bridges over the canal at Weston Point. Be did not know whether they would reach the one in West-road this year , but they would commence the one in Post Office-road at once. The bridges would be in the form of fixed bridges as the present type of swing bridge was net required, and he might also mention that they purposed carrying the railway siding over the latter bridge to Messrs. Castner Kellner's Works. In their operations they would interfere with the roadway as little as possible, and if they had to stop the roadway it would he only for a 17 days.

THE NEW cainuteN.

Mr. Kidd moved the appointm.ut of Mr. C. E Linaker as chairman of the Parma Council tor the ensuing year. Mr. Spencer seconded. Mr. Shore thought they should not overlook the quali- fications of Mr. Earlam, their vice-chairman. He was one of the oldest members of the Council with the excep- tion of himself, and he considered with all due respect to Mr. Linaker they ought to appoint him (Mr. Earlam) chairman. He moved his appointment. Mr. Illidge seconded. __ • _ . . . _

Mr. Earlam thought they should remember that by having Mr. Linaker as Chairman of the Council, they would be more in touch with the affairs of the Runcorn Rural District Council. Mr. Booth moved Mr. J. Moseley Williams as chair- man. He pointed out that Mr. Vb Mims was nominated by the late Mr. H. E. Heywood, but the nomination paper was mislaid. It was Mr. fleywood's wish that he should be on the Coancil.

No one seconded this and on a vote being taken Mr. Linaker was elected by eight votes to five. Mr. Linaker on taking ttic ehair Said he would have been equally pleased if Mr. Earlam had seen fit to take the position. Mr. Earlam had made an excellent chair- man in the absence of Mr. Heywood. He was sure r.o one could make a more efficient chairman than he. OTHER AEPOIRTMENTS.
The Chairman proP;sediand--hii::-Rodgers seconded, the re-appointment of Mr. Earlam as vice-cluirman.— Messrs. C. E. Linaker and J. W. Rothwell were reelected overseers of the poor. . . .

Mr. Linaker said he was very glad to observe that so far as the collection of the rates was concerned the township was ia a much better state than it hal been for some years.—Mr. W. B. Frith of Parr's Bank, Limited, was re-elected treasurer an the motion of Mr. Shore seconded by Mr. Earlam.—The following council- lors were elected as the Footpath Committee :—Messrs. div.head: THR CIIARITIES.
div.p: THR CIIARITIES.

'the Chairman said there were charities in the town- ship but they were not connected with the Parish Coun- cil. They were practically church charities. It was quite true that the recipients of one charity of which he (the chairman) was trustee, should be, according to the trust, church women not in receipt of parish relief, and tbey should also be regular in their attendances at divine worship. So far as he was cmcerned these strict regu- lations had not been adhered to. Widows were always selected who were not in receipt of parish relief and no difference was made whether they went to church or chapel. Then there was the Harrison charity which was distributed by the Ticar and Churchwardens on Christ- mas Day. The Grammar Schools was a charity in one sense, but it was only in respect to the payment of the income to the trustees. The charity with which he was connected was called the Upton Bequest. The money was left to be given away and they were ad- vised ny counsel that they ought to give it away as it stood (the bulk). Neither himself nor the late Dr. Roh- -1 inson could see their way to do that. The money was now invested and distributed on New Year's Day,but any balance would be held for any case if emergency. For instance, if any person were sick in the district there would always be some little aid forthcoming. What he proposed to do in future was to distribute a small por- tion of money at Christmas Sr New Year's Day. If there was a sum of say £lO or £l5 a woman might be set lup in business and by doing that they would be keeping iher off the rates, and she would be earning her own livelihood. He (Mr. Linaker) thought it a stupid idea to leave money in the way these bequests were made. The income was something like £450, and according to the terms of the bequest they might distribute the whole of the money among three or four persons. The only other charity was the Organ Charity which was purely ecclesi- astic, and the income thereof was devoted to the pay- ment of the organist's salary.

The Chairman esid that would be a question for the ParoelNal Committee to deal with.
During some rrrrrrrrrrr discussion on the subject, Mr.

Youd observed that if they had one of these oil cartgoing about the streets people would think they bad gone mad. (Loud laughter.) It was eventually decided to write Mr. J. Ashtetli clerk to the Rural District Council, on the matter.

NIGILECT OF CHILDREN.—SamueI and Annie Yarwoodi- husband and wife, of 35, Volunteer-street, Frodshantr were summoned for neglecting their four children in a. manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering, esi the sth April and ether dates within the past 6 month& Mr. I. W. Knowles, of Widnes, prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C.—lnspector McAteer said that in conse- quence of information received at Warrington,he visited Frodsham, and in company with Sergeant Clays and P.C. Price he went to the defendants house and saw the' four children Frederick 13 years,Thomas 8, Harry ,and Clara six menthe. He examined the children separately,- and found them all insufficiently clothed and filthy IS the extreme. Frederick was dressed in an old pair of pants and a pair of old clogs. He had no shirt on but what answered was the remains of a woman's old bodice.• When this was opened it was literally filled with vermin.. When the woman's attention was called to the condition' of the child she merely picked up the vermin and killed them in the presence of himself and the other officers. The other children were dressed in a similar condition.. Harry's body appeared to have been well bitten with vermin. The youngest child was dressed in a few old- rags which were saturated with urine. The back of the Child was covered with vermin bites, and it wall' In a delicate and thoroughly emaciated conditions The house was in a most filthy condition. There were mattresses on each bed but no bedding. On the chil- dren's bed there was only an old sack for the covsring. The only food in the house was one crust of bread. Asked to account for the state of things, defendant said he had done his best. It was due to drink. Witness. called at the house on the 19th inst., but no change had taken place. The children appeared to be fairly well nourished. The average wages going into the house amounted 303. a week. Other evidence having been given. the magistrates imposed a fine of 20s. including costs on, each of the defendants, or in default 14 days each with hard labour 'Sarah Morris and her husband, of Church Street, Frodsham, were also summoned for a like offence on the mine date. The husband did not appear. The evidence adduced in this case showed that the des fendants sriire charged with neglecting their five chils dren, Berne 9 years, Ethel 6, Ada 4, Mary Elizabeth and Thomas aged two years respectively. When the inspeC-- tor visited the house he found the parents out and all the children in with the oxception of Ada. The home wad destitute. There was nothing in the house but a small table and in one corner of the room there was a tick rolled up, which, when unrolled gave out a very often- MVO smell. There was no bed covering whatever, Be saw the mother at tse gr' ndmother's house in Main-- street, and vibes questioneJ she said her husband (mused 351, and sometimes £2 a week. He gave her 10s. and 15s. and sometimes less,a week. She said she was obliged to leave her husband a short time ago and he then sold all the furniture. The clothing the children wore durinS the day was taken off them at nights and these were' used as the bedclothes. The childeren were very poorly clad. A warrant was issued for the apprehension of the husband, and the case against the woman was allowed to stand over until the man was arrested. SODDEN DEATIE OF TEE HELM( POSTMASTER c IM- MOF.ST.—Au inquest was held by Mr. J. C. Batessoroner. for West Cheshire, at the Railway Inn, Helsby,on Feder on the body of John White, postmaster in the village. It transpired that on Wednesday evening, about nine o'clock, the deceased's wife, accompanied by Miss Sal- ford, the telegraphist, went out for a walk. They re.- turned about ten o'clock, and knocked at the door,- which was fastened. The deceased, who was in tbe house, called out "All right I will open the door." When he was on the point of opening the dcor Mrs. White arid Miss Salford heard him fall. They suosk the door, and then obtained the assistance of a man named Poole, wise suu,:eeded in gaining entrance to the house by the win- dow. On entering the house Poole observed the deceased on the floor, and when he removed him he discovered that he was apparently dead. Dr. Breast was iminedr- ately summoned, add on his arrival he pronoono3d life extinct. The deceased had complained for some weete' of having been in a poor state of healtb.—The jury re* turned a verdict of" Death from natural causes, pre- bably heart disease." The affair has caused some con' sternation in the district, Mr. White being well knots* and highly respected. Much sympathy is expressed for the widow in her painful bereavement.
